passages.text: Although a spotted hyena is smaller than a lion, the bite force of a hyena is greater than ______ lion of comparable age, allowing it to crack bones that lions usually leave behind.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Coating tests
passages.text: In the laboratory, one group of engineers sprayed salt water on coated steel panels every hour for six weeks. ______ a second group placed identical panels on a pier by the ocean and checked them once a week for rust.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Fresco notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A fifteenth-century fresco covers the walls of a small chapel in central Italy.
• Conservators began restoring it in 2009.
• They removed centuries of grime by hand, a few square centimeters at a time.
• The restoration was completed in 2021.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bacteria experiment
passages.text: Because the samples had been contaminated during shipping ______ the team discarded them and repeated the entire experiment with fresh cultures.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Steps by season
passages.text:
A study measured the average number of steps taken per day by adults in three age groups during summer and winter.
Age group | Summer | Winter
20–39 | 8,200 | 7,600
40–59 | 7,500 | 6,700
60 and older | 6,400 | 4,800
The researchers claim that the drop in daily steps from summer to winter was largest for adults aged 60 and older.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The rehearsal
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story.
The orchestra had rehearsed the symphony's final movement eleven times that week. On the twelfth run, the conductor lowered her baton halfway through, said nothing for a long moment, and then told the musicians to go home early. Several of them looked at one another, unsure whether they had played very badly or very well.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A trial semester
passages.text: When the school board reviewed the proposal to keep the public library open until 9 p.m., its response was ______: members praised the plan's goals but voted to fund only a one-semester trial before committing to a permanent change.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Beaten thin
passages.text: Gold is unusually ______: a single gram of it can be hammered into a sheet nearly one square meter in area without tearing, a property that has made gold leaf a favorite of artists and bookbinders for centuries.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Worms that came later
passages.text: For much of the twentieth century, many gardeners and naturalists in the northern United States and Canada assumed that the earthworms in local forests had always lived there. Studies of species and their histories, however, indicate that most earthworms in these northern forests arrived from Europe and Asia in soil and plants carried by settlers, because the glaciers of the last ice age had largely wiped out native earthworms in the region. Ecologists now study how these newcomers alter the leaf litter and soil of forests that developed without them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Narrow rings
passages.text: Researchers examining tree rings in a mountain valley found that pines on dry, south-facing slopes formed unusually narrow rings for an entire decade in the 1800s. Pines of the same species growing beside the valley's river, where groundwater is always available, formed rings of normal width during the same decade. These findings suggest that the narrow rings most likely reflect ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three gardens
passages.text:
A city tracked three community gardens during one growing season.
Garden | Number of plots | Total harvest (kg)
A | 40 | 2,000
B | 25 | 1,500
C | 15 | 1,050
A city report claims that Garden C was the most productive per plot even though it had the fewest plots.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A farmer's find
passages.text: The silver coins, ______ in 1903 by a farmer plowing a field near the river, are now displayed at the county museum alongside the farmer's own account of the discovery.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three generations
passages.text: Marisol Vega's 2015 novel The Orchards ______ the story of three generations of a family who run a fruit farm in central California, moving back and forth among their perspectives.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A fish without eyes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Ozark cavefish is a small, pale fish with no functional eyes.
• It lives in caves and underground streams.
• Its range is limited to parts of Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
• It is listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Eleven prototypes
passages.text: Although her first designs failed every field test, the engineer remained ______, rebuilding and retesting the water filter eleven times over three years until it finally met the village council's standard.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Weighing two readings
passages.text: Reviewers praised the historian's account of the 1848 uprising as ______: it lays out the strengths of both rival interpretations of the event before cautiously favoring one of them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lights on the beach
passages.text: Newly hatched sea turtles find the ocean by heading toward the brightest part of the horizon, which on an undeveloped beach is usually the open sky above the water. Along developed coastlines, however, streetlights and lit windows can be brighter than the sea, and hatchlings may crawl inland, where many die. In response, a number of coastal towns now require residents to shield or turn off outdoor lights visible from the beach during nesting season.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Folding leaves
passages.text: Botanist Lena Ortiz hypothesizes that a desert shrub folds its leaves in the hottest part of the day mainly to reduce the amount of water the leaves lose.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A quieter motor
passages.text: After two years of development, the appliance maker announced that ______ new electric motor for washing machines runs about 40 percent more quietly than the model it replaces.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An old crossing
passages.text: The Fennick River ferry carried passengers and freight for nearly a century before the county built a bridge at the same crossing in 1931, ______ remains in daily use and was widened in 1978.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A field without a plow
passages.text: For generations, farmers in the region prepared their fields each spring by plowing the soil deeply. ______ a growing number now plant directly into the stubble of the previous crop, a practice that leaves the soil undisturbed and helps it hold water.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Glass frogs
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Glass frogs live in the rainforests of Central and South America.
• Many have skin on their undersides so transparent that their hearts and other organs are visible.
• When glass frogs sleep, most of their red blood cells move into the liver.
• This makes the frogs about two to three times more transparent while they rest.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Listening plants
passages.text: Some plants appear to respond to the vibrations made by insects feeding on them. ______ in one experiment, thale cress plants that had been exposed to recorded vibrations of caterpillars chewing produced more of a defensive chemical when caterpillars later fed on them than plants that had not been exposed to such vibrations did.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Who has seen the wind?
passages.text: "Who Has Seen the Wind?" is an 1872 poem by Christina Rossetti. In the poem, the speaker suggests that the wind's presence can be known through its effects on the natural world.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Brief blooms
passages.text: Some desert wildflowers are strikingly ______: after a rare heavy rain they sprout, bloom, and drop their seeds within a few weeks, then disappear from the landscape until the next downpour, which may be years away.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A cautious announcement
passages.text: In interviews about her team's discovery, the astronomer's tone was notably ______: she called the result "interesting" rather than "groundbreaking" and repeatedly stressed how much remained unknown.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Safety in numbers
passages.text: Periodical cicadas in parts of North America spend 13 or 17 years underground as nymphs and then emerge by the millions within a few weeks. This timing is not a coincidence. Birds and other predators can eat only a small fraction of such an enormous swarm, so most of the cicadas survive long enough to mate, a strategy biologists call predator satiation.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A regular dip
passages.text: Astronomers observing a distant star found that its brightness dropped by the same small amount every 12.4 days, with each dip lasting about three hours. Random changes on a star's surface do not repeat on such a precise schedule. The astronomers therefore concluded that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Litter by type
passages.text:
Volunteers counted the litter collected during an annual beach cleanup. The town banned single-use plastic bags in 2022.
Litter type | 2021 | 2023
Plastic bottles | 420 | 210
Cigarette butts | 650 | 600
Plastic bags | 300 | 90
A local report claims that, from 2021 to 2023, plastic bags showed the largest percentage decrease of any litter type in the table.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: One hand or two? (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A historian argues that a fourteenth-century manuscript of sermons was copied entirely by a single scribe, citing the remarkably consistent shape of the letters from the first page to the last.

Text 2
Scribes trained in the same workshop were taught to imitate a single house style so closely that their hands can be hard to tell apart. In this manuscript, analysis of the parchment shows that the last third was made from animal skins prepared differently from those used in the first two-thirds.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Mountain pastures
passages.text: Each spring, the ______ of the valley drive their goats up to the high pastures, where the animals graze until the first snow.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Above all
passages.text: The expedition's success depended on one thing more than any other ______ the weather in the narrow window when the pass would be free of ice.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Inefficient but indispensable
passages.text: The earliest steam engines were enormously inefficient, turning only a tiny fraction of the energy in their fuel into useful work. ______ they transformed mining in eighteenth-century Britain, because they could pump water out of deep mines far faster than teams of horses could.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Refill stations
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2023, Ridgeview High School installed four water-bottle refill stations.
• Sales of bottled water in Ridgeview's cafeteria fell by 40 percent that year.
• Each station cost about $1,500 to install.
• The district's two other high schools have no refill stations.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: One shared style
passages.text: The proposed link between the two ancient settlements remains ______: it rests entirely on a single shared pottery style, which could just as easily have spread between unrelated communities through trade.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Slow gains
passages.text: Rather than arriving in a sudden breakthrough, the improvement in phone battery life over the past decade has been ______, with each new generation lasting only slightly longer than the one before it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A risky descent
passages.text: Three-toed sloths spend nearly all their lives in trees, yet about once a week they climb down to the ground to defecate, a trip that exposes them to predators. Researchers have found that moths living in sloth fur lay their eggs in the dung. The moths later return to the fur, where they appear to add nutrients that help algae grow there, and sloths sometimes eat that algae. Based on these findings, the researchers proposed that the risky descent ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three wheat varieties
passages.text:
Researchers grew three varieties of wheat on 10 farms and recorded each variety's yield, in metric tons per hectare.
Variety | Average yield | Lowest yield | Highest yield
A | 4.1 | 3.8 | 4.4
B | 4.3 | 3.6 | 4.9
C | 4.6 | 2.9 | 6.0
The researchers claim that variety C produced the highest yields on average but was also the least consistent from farm to farm.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Composed on the spot? (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
A music critic describes jazz improvisation as composition in its purest form: a soloist invents an entirely new melody in the moment, with nothing prepared in advance.

Text 2
Studies of recorded jazz solos have found that experienced players frequently reuse short melodic phrases, often called licks, that they practiced beforehand. Skilled improvisers combine and vary these familiar phrases in new ways as they respond to the music around them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A first program
passages.text: Ada Lovelace, a mathematician by ______ wrote in 1843 a set of notes on a proposed calculating machine that included what many historians consider the first published computer program.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Sold out
passages.text: By noon the bakery had sold every loaf of bread ______ by evening, even the last tray of pastries was gone.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Trees and fire
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The cones of lodgepole pines are often sealed with resin that melts in the heat of a fire, releasing seeds onto the burned ground.
• Jack pines also have cones that open mainly after exposure to fire.
• Some eucalyptus trees sprout new shoots from buds under their bark after a fire.
• All three kinds of trees grow in places where wildfires occur regularly.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Prices without minutes
passages.text: No rule in the guild's charter forbade members from undercutting one another's prices, yet historians believe members observed a ______ understanding on the matter: the records of guild meetings never mention prices at all, but members' prices stayed within a few pennies of one another for decades.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A small jaw
passages.text: The fossil's modest size ______ its significance: the jaw, barely two centimeters long, preserves a pattern of tooth replacement that researchers had predicted for fish of its age but had never before observed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A relay across generations
passages.text: Each fall, monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly thousands of kilometers to forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter. In spring they head north, but no individual completes the return. The butterflies breed along the way, and it is their children and grandchildren that continue the journey and reach the northern United States and Canada. The monarchs that fly south again in the fall may therefore be the great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico in spring.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Urban coyotes
passages.text: Food from people, such as garbage and pet food, is plentiful in cities and takes little effort for coyotes to obtain, so one might expect urban coyotes that eat it to be healthier than coyotes that hunt. A 2015 study in Edmonton, Canada, found the reverse: coyotes whose diets included more human food were in poorer body condition and more likely to have mange. One possible explanation is that human food, though plentiful, is low in the protein that coyotes need, which would mean that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Window treatments
passages.text:
Researchers recorded the average number of bird collisions per month at office buildings before and after one of three window treatments was installed.
Treatment | Before | After
Dot-pattern film | 20 | 6
UV-reflective glass | 40 | 22
Exterior netting | 10 | 4
The researchers concluded that, relative to each building group's starting level, the dot-pattern film was the most effective of the three treatments.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Following a point (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In experiments where a person points to one of two cups hiding food, pet dogs choose the correct cup far more often than chimpanzees do. Some researchers have concluded that domestication gave dogs an inborn sensitivity to human gestures that their wild relatives lack.
Text 2
Other researchers have found that wolves raised by people from birth can follow pointing about as well as pet dogs, while shelter dogs with little human contact often struggle with the task. These researchers argue that a dog's experience with people shapes this skill more than has been recognized.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Twelve receptors
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Humans have three types of color photoreceptors.
• Mantis shrimp have twelve types of color photoreceptors.
• Researchers expected mantis shrimp to tell apart very similar colors.
• In a 2014 study, mantis shrimp could not reliably distinguish colors that people can easily tell apart.
• The researchers suggested that the shrimp may identify colors directly instead of comparing signals from different receptors.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Otters and kelp
passages.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins, and where otters have returned to the coast, urchin numbers have dropped and kelp forests have regrown. ______ the otters' appetite for crabs and clams has brought them into conflict with people who harvest those animals for food.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An unread manuscript
passages.text: The Voynich manuscript, a fifteenth-century book written in an unknown ______ has resisted every attempt at decipherment, including efforts by professional codebreakers during the twentieth century.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A contaminated plate
passages.text: In September 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from a vacation and found that a mold had contaminated one of the culture plates in his laboratory. He noticed that the mold growing on the plate ______ the bacteria immediately around it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Draupner wave
passages.text: For decades, sailors' reports of "rogue waves" (single waves more than twice as tall as the surrounding seas) were often dismissed as exaggerations, since standard models predicted that such waves should be extremely rare. Then, on January 1, 1995, a laser sensor on the Draupner oil platform in the North Sea recorded a wave about 26 meters high amid seas of roughly 12 meters. Researchers have since revised their models, and satellite surveys suggest rogue waves are more common than once believed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A faithful restoration
passages.text: The restored theater is ______ its 1920s original: the architects reproduced the painted ceiling and gilded balconies exactly, altering only the wiring and plumbing hidden behind the walls.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Returning the collection
passages.text: The museum's offer to return the carved masks to the community that made them was ______: the museum would send the masks only after the community had built climate-controlled storage for them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Giant tortoises
passages.text: Fossil sites on an island show that a species of giant tortoise disappeared at about the same time humans first arrived there. Some researchers have concluded that human hunting drove the tortoises to extinction. However, pollen preserved at the same sites shows that the island's climate became drier during that period and that the plants the tortoises ate declined sharply. Thus, the timing of human arrival alone ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Crows and a park
passages.text: Crows in one city avoid a particular park, even though it contains trees and food sources similar to those in parks the crows visit often. A researcher hypothesizes that the crows avoid the park because, years earlier, a scientist trapped and banded crows there, and the birds have come to associate the place with danger, not because of any feature of the park itself.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Dusty panels
passages.text:
Researchers measured the output of solar panels under three cleaning schedules in the dry season and in the rainy season. Output is given as a percent of the panels' maximum possible output.
Cleaning schedule | Dry season | Rainy season
Weekly | 96 | 97
Monthly | 88 | 95
Never | 75 | 93
The researchers concluded that cleaning makes a much larger difference to output in the dry season than in the rainy season.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Monsters at sea (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
The sea serpents and whales that decorate many medieval and Renaissance maps have often been read as warnings. On this view, mapmakers drew monsters in waters they considered dangerous or poorly known, telling sailors, in effect, to beware.
Text 2
A historian of cartography who traced many of these creatures to the natural-history books of the period argues that mapmakers usually believed such animals really lived where they drew them. The creatures, he suggests, were often a way of recording what was thought to be known about the oceans, and of showing off the mapmaker's skill, more than a way of marking danger.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Underground canals
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A qanat is an underground channel that carries groundwater from the foot of a mountain to fields or towns.
• Water flows through a qanat by gravity alone.
• Qanats were first built in what is now Iran roughly 3,000 years ago.
• Because the water travels underground, much less of it evaporates than in an open canal.
• Builders dug a series of vertical shafts and then connected them with a gently sloping tunnel.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An unusual eruption
passages.text: Most large volcanic eruptions cool the planet for a year or two, because the sulfur dioxide they release forms tiny particles that reflect sunlight. The 2022 eruption of the underwater volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai released relatively little sulfur dioxide. ______ it blasted an enormous amount of water vapor, a heat-trapping gas, into the upper atmosphere, leading some scientists to suggest that it might temporarily warm the planet rather than cool it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three stops
passages.text: The research vessel's three stops on its North Atlantic voyage were Reykjavík, ______ Nuuk, Greenland; and Iqaluit, Canada.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Mission Blue
passages.text: The oceanographer Sylvia Earle, who has led more than a hundred expeditions and spent thousands of hours underwater over her career, ______ the organization Mission Blue in 2009 to promote the creation of protected areas in the ocean.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A partial skeleton
passages.text: The new dinosaur species was described from a single ______ specimen: the skeleton lacked its skull and most of its tail, so researchers could estimate the animal's length only roughly.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A decisive speech
passages.text: Before the senator spoke, the bill's supporters had seemed divided and unsure. Her speech ______ them: many who had wavered announced their support the next morning, and the bill passed within the week.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seen from orbit
passages.text: Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can easily be seen from space with the naked eye. Astronauts who have looked for it from low orbit report that it is very hard to pick out. Although the wall is extremely long, it is only a few meters wide and is built from materials close in color to the land around it. Highways and airport runways, which are wider and contrast more with their surroundings, are far easier to spot.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Fish in the forest
passages.text: Pacific salmon spend most of their lives in the ocean but return to rivers to spawn and die. Bears catch many of them and often carry the carcasses into the woods to eat. Researchers have found that leaves of trees growing beside salmon streams are unusually rich in a heavy form of nitrogen that is relatively more abundant in ocean life than in land ecosystems, and that such trees can grow faster than trees of the same species beside streams without salmon. These findings suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two kinds of visits
passages.text:
A museum surveyed visitors in four age groups about how they had experienced its collection in the past year.
Age group | Visited in person | Took a virtual tour
18–29 | 45% | 38%
30–49 | 52% | 31%
50–64 | 48% | 22%
65 and older | 55% | 14%
A researcher concluded that the gap between in-person visits and virtual tours is much wider among the oldest visitors than among the youngest.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rising at the end (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In many varieties of English, some speakers end statements with a rise in pitch, as if asking a question. Critics of this habit, often called uptalk, argue that it signals uncertainty and makes speakers sound less confident than they are.
Text 2
Linguists who have analyzed recorded conversations report that speakers often use this rising pitch on statements they are clearly sure of, such as when giving directions or listing facts. In those settings, the rise seems to work as a check, inviting the listener to signal that they are following.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A raven's plan
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In a 2017 study, researchers taught ravens to use a stone tool to open a box containing food.
• Later, with the box out of sight, each raven was offered the tool among several useless objects.
• Most ravens picked the tool and kept it.
• The researchers tested delays of 15 minutes and of 17 hours before returning the box.
• When the box was returned, as much as 17 hours later, the ravens used the tool to open it.
• Planning for a future need is rare among animals.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Not quite emission-free
passages.text: Electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions. ______ manufacturing their batteries takes a great deal of energy, much of which still comes from burning fossil fuels, so the cars are not emission-free over their full lives.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Found in a bog
passages.text: Excavated from a peat bog in Denmark in 1950, ______ so well preserved that the people who found it first thought they had come upon a recent crime.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Delayed reopening
passages.text: The bridge had been scheduled to reopen in ______ repairs to its suspension cables took longer than engineers expected, and it remained closed until August.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A spreading vine
passages.text: Once found only in a few gardens, the vine has become ______ in the region: it now grows along nearly every roadside, fence line and riverbank.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A plan with room to grow
passages.text: The architects' plan for the new campus was deliberately ______: by leaving large parts of the site unbuilt and designing roads that could be extended, it allowed the city to add buildings as future needs became clear.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Grains from a geyser
passages.text: Plumes of water vapor erupting from Saturn's moon Enceladus contain salt and tiny grains of silica. On Earth, silica grains of that size typically form when water that is hot enough to dissolve rock cools rapidly. Researchers studying the plumes therefore concluded that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A snail that stops flinching
passages.text: When a garden snail is tapped lightly on its shell, it pulls back into the shell. After many harmless taps in a row, however, it stops withdrawing. A biologist hypothesizes that the snail has learned that the taps are harmless, rather than simply becoming too tired to withdraw.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lamps and insects
passages.text:
Researchers placed insect traps beneath three kinds of outdoor lighting for one summer and counted the insects caught per trap each night.
Lighting | Average insects per trap per night
White LED lamp | 120
Amber LED lamp | 45
No lamp | 10
The researchers concluded that switching from white to amber lamps would greatly reduce, but not eliminate, the extra insects that outdoor lighting attracts.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The end of Norse Greenland (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Norse settlers lived in Greenland for nearly five hundred years before their settlements were abandoned in the 1400s. Many historians have attributed the abandonment mainly to a cooling climate, which shortened growing seasons and made it harder to keep livestock.
Text 2
Other historians point out that the settlements depended heavily on exporting walrus ivory to Europe. As European demand for walrus ivory fell in the 1300s and 1400s, they argue, the settlements lost the trade that had paid for imported goods, leaving them less able to withstand hard years.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A blast over Siberia
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• On June 30, 1908, a huge explosion occurred over a remote forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia.
• It flattened an estimated 80 million trees over more than 2,000 square kilometers.
• Scientists reached the area for the first time in 1927.
• They expected to find a crater made by a meteorite but found none.
• Most scientists now think a space rock exploded in the air above the forest before it could reach the ground.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A library built for efficiency
passages.text: The new public library was designed to use far less energy than the building it replaced. ______ its roof is covered with solar panels, and its windows are angled to let in low winter sunlight while blocking the higher summer sun.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A fish from the deep past
passages.text: The ______ a fish once thought to have died out with the dinosaurs—was found alive off the coast of South Africa in 1938.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A council's decision
passages.text: The city council approved the new budget last week, but ______ decision to reduce library hours drew protests from parents and teachers.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A dependable spring
passages.text: The village's water supply had always seemed ______: even in the driest summers, the spring at the edge of town kept flowing as strongly as ever.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Test wells
passages.text: The first season's results were ______: three of the four test wells drilled in the valley struck water, suggesting that the larger irrigation project could succeed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Concrete that mends itself
passages.text: Ancient Roman concrete often contains small white lumps of lime, which researchers long assumed were signs of careless mixing. A 2023 study suggested a different explanation. When cracks form and water seeps in, the lumps can dissolve and then harden again as a new mineral that fills the cracks. The lumps, in other words, may have helped some Roman structures repair their own damage over the centuries.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Remembering the board
passages.text: In a classic study, chess experts and beginners were briefly shown chessboards and then asked to reconstruct them from memory. When the pieces were arranged as they might appear in a real game, the experts recalled far more of them than the beginners did. When the pieces were placed at random, however, the experts did only slightly better than the beginners. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: How far seeds travel
passages.text:
Researchers tracked how far two bird species carried the seeds of a fruiting tree before dropping them.
Bird species | Median distance (meters) | Longest distance recorded (meters)
Species A | 120 | 400
Species B | 60 | 900
The researchers concluded that species A usually carries seeds farther than species B does, but that species B occasionally carries seeds much farther than species A ever did.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes by hand (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
In a widely cited 2014 study, students who took lecture notes by hand answered conceptual questions about the lecture better than students who typed notes on laptops. The researchers suggested that writing by hand, which is slower, forces students to summarize ideas rather than copy words, and so improves learning.
Text 2
Later researchers repeated the study's procedures with new groups of students. They found that differences between handwritten and typed notes were smaller and less consistent than originally reported, and in several comparisons there was no reliable difference at all.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Training abroad
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Bessie Coleman wanted to become a pilot in the early 1920s.
• Flight schools in the United States refused to admit her because she was Black and a woman.
• She learned French and traveled to France to train.
• In 1921 she earned an international pilot's license there.
• She returned to the United States and performed in air shows.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Water and storms
passages.text: Warm ocean water supplies the heat and moisture that power a hurricane, which is why storms often strengthen as they cross warm seas. ______ a hurricane that stalls over one area can churn up cooler water from below the surface, cutting off its own supply of warmth and weakening itself.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Singing at the festival
passages.text: The ______ performance was the highlight of the town's spring festival, drawing a larger crowd than any of the professional acts.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Building a dam
passages.text: Construction of Hoover Dam began in 1931. By the time the dam was completed in 1936, thousands of workers ______ on the project, often in extreme desert heat.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A field clinic
passages.text: After the flood cut the town's only road, volunteers set up a ______ clinic in the school gym: folding tables served as examination beds, bedsheets hung from volleyball nets divided the patients, and car batteries powered the lamps.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An early warning
passages.text: In 1896, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling the carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere would warm the planet by several degrees. Most of his contemporaries thought the effect too small or too distant to matter, but measurements taken more than a century later suggest that his basic conclusion was ______.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A brainless network
passages.text: The slime mold Physarum polycephalum is a single cell with no brain or nervous system. In one experiment, researchers placed oat flakes, a food the mold seeks out, on a dish in a pattern matching the locations of cities around Tokyo. The mold first spread across the dish and then pulled back, leaving a network of tubes connecting the food sources that closely resembled the region's actual rail system. Engineers have since studied how the mold builds such networks for ideas about designing efficient transportation and communication systems.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Walking statues
passages.text: The moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) are stone statues, many weighing several tons, that were moved long distances from the quarry where they were carved. Because the island had few large trees when Europeans arrived, some researchers doubted that the statues could have been dragged lying down on wooden sledges, which would have required large amounts of timber. Island oral traditions say that the moai "walked" to their platforms. In 2012, researchers tied ropes to the head of an upright concrete replica and, by rocking it from side to side, moved it about 100 meters in under an hour with a team of 18 people. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Phones and braking
passages.text:
In a driving-simulator study, researchers measured how long participants took to brake after a car ahead of them stopped suddenly.
Condition | Average reaction time (seconds)
No phone call | 0.9
Hands-free phone call | 1.3
Handheld phone call | 1.4
The researchers concluded that hands-free calls slow drivers' reactions nearly as much as handheld calls do.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Listening with their feet
passages.text: Elephants produce low rumbling calls, and the vibrations from these calls travel through the ground as well as through the air. Biologist Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell hypothesized that elephants can detect such ground vibrations and respond to them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Hedy Lamarr's invention
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hedy Lamarr was a film actress who also worked on inventions.
• In 1942, she and the composer George Antheil received a patent for a "secret communication system."
• The system rapidly switched a radio signal among 88 frequencies.
• Its purpose was to keep enemies from jamming the radio signals used to guide torpedoes.
• The number 88 matched the number of keys on a piano.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rocks from Mars
passages.text: Most meteorites found on Earth are fragments of asteroids. ______ a small number come from Mars: gases trapped inside them closely match the Martian atmosphere as measured by the Viking landers in 1976.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A three-port voyage
passages.text: On its first voyage, the steamship called at three ports along the Pacific coast of South America: Valparaíso, Chile; Callao, Peru______ Guayaquil, Ecuador.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A ferry safety rule
passages.text: After an inspection found that several life jackets on the island ferry had been stored behind locked panels, the harbor authority required that every vessel ______ its safety equipment where passengers can reach it without tools.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Early automobiles
passages.text: In 1900, the American automobile industry was still ______: only about eight thousand cars were registered in the entire country, and most were built by hand in small workshops.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A modest architect
passages.text: Although she designed several of the city's best-known buildings, the architect was notably ______: she drove an old car, ate lunch with the junior drafters, and credited her colleagues whenever her work won an award.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Burrs and fasteners
passages.text: In 1941, the Swiss engineer George de Mestral returned from a walk to find burrs clinging to his trousers and to his dog's fur. Curious, he examined a burr under a microscope and saw that it was covered in tiny hooks that caught on anything with loops, such as fabric or hair. It took him years to reproduce the effect with woven nylon. The result, a fastener made of one strip of hooks and one of loops, was patented in the 1950s under the name Velcro.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The new coat
passages.text:
The following text is from an original short story. Ana has just received a winter coat from her older sister, Marisol.
The coat was the deep green of pine needles, and it still smelled faintly of Marisol's perfume. One cuff had been carefully mended with thread that almost matched. Ana had wanted a new coat all autumn, one with shiny buttons that no one else had worn. Now she turned the green coat over in her hands, found the mended cuff, and pictured her sister bent over it late at night. She put the coat on and did not take it off for the rest of the day.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seedlings and parent trees
passages.text:
In one tropical forest, researchers tracked the survival of seedlings of a single tree species for two years, grouping them by distance from the nearest adult tree of the same species.
Distance from adult tree | Seedlings that survived two years
0–5 meters | 12%
5–20 meters | 35%
More than 20 meters | 51%
The researchers concluded that seedlings growing close to an adult of their own species are less likely to survive than seedlings growing farther away.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Patient cuttlefish
passages.text: Researchers offered common cuttlefish a choice: a piece of king prawn available right away, or a live grass shrimp, which cuttlefish prefer, that would be released only after a delay. Many cuttlefish ignored the prawn and waited for the shrimp, some for more than a minute. The cuttlefish that waited longest also learned a separate task more quickly than the others did. Because self-control and learning ability seemed to go together in these animals, the researchers suggested that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The guilty look (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Many dog owners report that their dogs look "guilty"—lowering their heads, avoiding eye contact, and tucking their tails—after doing something forbidden. To many owners, this look shows that dogs know when they have broken a rule.
Text 2
In a 2009 study, psychologist Alexandra Horowitz told owners to forbid their dogs from eating a treat and then leave the room. Sometimes the dogs ate the treat; sometimes the researcher secretly removed it. Owners were then told, sometimes falsely, that their dog had eaten it. Dogs showed the most "guilty" behavior when their owners scolded them, whether or not the dog had actually eaten the treat.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The Golden Records
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft were launched in 1977.
• Each carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record.
• The records contain greetings in 55 languages, natural sounds, music, and 115 images encoded in sound.
• They were intended as a message to any intelligent beings who might someday find the spacecraft.
• Both spacecraft have since left the region of space dominated by the solar wind.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A helpful robot
passages.text: The warehouse robot can climb short flights of stairs, open doors with a gripper arm, and ______ packages weighing up to twenty kilograms.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Discovering a signal
passages.text: The astronomer ______ team first detected the repeating radio signal was initially reluctant to announce the finding until other observatories had confirmed it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An odd reading
passages.text: Most of the probe's temperature readings fell within the range engineers had predicted, but one reading from the sensor near the antenna was so far outside that range that the team at first suspected a faulty instrument rather than a real change. Engineers called the reading ______ and scheduled a second measurement to check it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Ordinary objects
passages.text: The photographer is known for turning ______ subjects into striking images: a dish rack, a parking meter, and a puddle reflecting a streetlight have all appeared in her prize-winning series.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Hummingbird nights
passages.text: Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of any bird, and a hummingbird can burn through its energy reserves overnight if it stays fully active. On cold nights, many hummingbirds enter torpor, a sleeplike state in which body temperature can fall by many degrees and heart rate slows dramatically. In this state, a bird uses only a small fraction of the energy it would otherwise need. Researchers studying hummingbirds high in the Andes have recorded body temperatures during torpor as low as about 3 degrees Celsius.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Mole-rat dialects
passages.text: Naked mole-rats live in underground colonies and greet one another with soft chirps. Researchers found that each colony's chirps share a distinct pattern, or dialect, and that mole-rats respond more strongly to chirps in their own colony's dialect. Pups moved to a different colony shortly after birth grew up producing the dialect of the colony that raised them, not the one they were born into. And when a colony's queen was removed, the colony's chirps became more varied, until a new queen took over and the calls grew similar again. These findings suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Watching hands
passages.text:
A hospital measured how often staff cleaned their hands when entering patients' rooms, using two methods over the same months.
Method | Hand-cleaning rate
Trained observer visibly present on the ward | 85%
Automated sensors, no observer present | 40%
Researchers concluded that rates recorded by visible observers likely overstate how often staff clean their hands when no one appears to be watching.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Remembering caches
passages.text: Clark's nutcrackers bury thousands of pine seeds in the fall and recover many of them months later. Biologist Stephen Vander Wall hypothesized that the birds find their caches by remembering the positions of nearby landmarks, such as rocks and logs, rather than by smell or by searching at random.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The bluestones (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some geologists have argued that the smaller "bluestones" at Stonehenge, which came from the Preseli Hills in Wales about 230 kilometers away, were carried most of the way to England by glaciers during an ice age, so that Stonehenge's builders had only to collect them nearby.
Text 2
Archaeologists led by Mike Parker Pearson excavated two outcrops in the Preseli Hills and found stone tools, wedges, and artificial platforms beneath the rock faces, along with hearths dated to around the time Stonehenge was built. They also found gaps in the outcrops that match the shapes of bluestones at Stonehenge.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Tu Youyou
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1969, the Chinese scientist Tu Youyou began searching for a new malaria treatment.
• Her team screened more than 2,000 traditional herbal remedies.
• A 1,600-year-old text described soaking sweet wormwood in cold water.
• Following that clue, Tu extracted the plant at a low temperature, which preserved its active compound, artemisinin.
• In 2015, she shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A slow method
passages.text: Radiocarbon dating requires destroying a small sample of the object being tested, and results can take weeks to arrive. ______ the method remains the standard for dating organic material up to about 50,000 years old, because no other technique matches its accuracy across that span.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A prolific director
passages.text: By the time the choir's founding director retired in 2019, she had ______ more than forty original pieces for the group, several of which are still performed every season.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A limited committee
passages.text: The new oversight committee's authority is notably ______: it may review the city's budget and recommend changes, but it cannot approve, reject, or delay any spending on its own.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An idea proved right
passages.text: When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined and had slowly drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea because he could not explain what force moved them. Half a century later, maps of the ocean floor revealed new crust forming along mid-ocean ridges and spreading outward, providing the mechanism Wegener had lacked. His central claim was ______ by evidence he never lived to see.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A fragile fruit
passages.text: Until the 1950s, most bananas sold in North America and Europe were of a single variety, the Gros Michel. Because commercial bananas are grown from cuttings rather than seeds, every Gros Michel plant was genetically almost identical to every other. When a soil fungus that causes Panama disease spread through plantations, no plants had natural resistance, and growers were forced to switch to a resistant variety, the Cavendish. Today the Cavendish dominates the export trade in the same way, and a new strain of the same fungus has begun to attack it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Crowded locusts
passages.text: Desert locusts usually live alone and avoid one another. When they are crowded together, however, they can switch within hours to a swarming form that seeks out other locusts and travels in huge groups. Researchers found that repeatedly touching the hind legs of solitary locusts triggered this switch and was accompanied by a sharp rise in serotonin, a chemical messenger in the nervous system. When locusts were given a drug that blocks serotonin's effects and then crowded together, they ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bats and streetlights
passages.text:
Researchers counted bat passes per night near experimental streetlights of three colors, separately for bat species that avoid light and species that hunt insects attracted to light.
Light condition | Light-avoiding species | Light-tolerant species
No light | 40 | 50
White light | 10 | 90
Red light | 36 | 55
The researchers concluded that red light let light-avoiding bats remain nearly as active as they were in darkness, unlike white light.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Language and direction (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal Australian language, describe locations using cardinal directions ("the cup is north of the plate") rather than words like "left" and "right." In tests, they keep track of compass directions with remarkable accuracy, even indoors. Some researchers conclude that the language people speak shapes how they think about space.
Text 2
Critics point out that communities using cardinal-direction languages often also live in landscapes and follow daily routines that demand constant attention to direction. In studies that compared people who speak the same language but live in different environments, sense of direction tracked environment and habits about as closely as it tracked language.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two space telescopes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990.
• Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
• The James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021.
• Webb observes mainly infrared light, which can pass through clouds of dust that block visible light.
• Webb orbits about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, much farther than Hubble.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A demanding vaccine
passages.text: ______ the new vaccine must be kept at temperatures far below freezing, which makes it difficult to deliver to remote clinics. In trials, however, it prevented about 95 percent of cases, a level of protection that health officials say justifies the extra effort.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An old question
passages.text: For centuries, naturalists were puzzled by a question that no one could answer with certainty: where do European eels go to spawn______ Not until the 1920s did researchers trace the youngest larvae to the Sargasso Sea.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A near miss
passages.text: Astronomers estimate that if the comet ______ even slightly closer to the Sun during its 2020 pass, the heat would probably have broken it apart.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A quick inspection
passages.text: The auditor's review of the contracts was ______: she glanced at the first page of each one and signed off without checking any of the figures inside.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Stalled talks
passages.text: After six weeks of negotiations, both sides remained ______: the union refused to lower its wage demand by even a single percentage point, and the company would not raise its offer at all.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Floating seeds
passages.text: A dandelion seed travels on a pappus, a tuft of about a hundred fine bristles. Engineers long assumed that such a sparse structure could not create much drag. In 2018, however, researchers using wind tunnels found that air flowing through the gaps between the bristles forms a stable ring of swirling air just above the seed, a kind of vortex that had not been described before. This ring slows the seed's fall, letting it drift for long distances while using very little material.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Washing potatoes
passages.text: In 1953, researchers on the Japanese island of Koshima saw a young female macaque named Imo wash a sandy sweet potato in a stream before eating it. Over the next few years, the behavior spread first to Imo's playmates and her mother, then to the playmates' mothers, and eventually to most of the troop. The adult males, who spent the least time near the young monkeys, were the slowest to adopt it, and some never did. This pattern suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shrinking ice
passages.text:
A lake's average number of ice-covered days per winter was recorded for four decades spread across more than a century.
Period | Average ice-covered days
1900s | 120
1950s | 110
2000s | 95
2010s | 88
A researcher claimed that ice cover has not only declined but has declined faster in recent decades than in the early twentieth century.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Roots and running water
passages.text: Plant roots grow toward moisture in the soil. Biologist Monica Gagliano wondered whether roots might also respond to the sound of water. She hypothesized that pea roots can grow toward the sound of flowing water even when no moisture difference guides them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Wolves and willows (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, willows along many streams began to recover. Some ecologists attributed this to a "landscape of fear": elk, wary of wolves, avoided lingering along open streambanks, so they browsed less on young willows.
Text 2
Later studies found that elk numbers in the park had also fallen because of hunting outside the park, growing populations of bears and cougars, and drought. In several areas, elk did not noticeably avoid risky streambanks, and willows recovered only where elk numbers had dropped sharply.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Wangari Maathai
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan biologist and environmental activist.
• In 1977, she founded the Green Belt Movement.
• The movement paid women in rural communities to plant trees.
• Its members have planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya.
• In 2004, Maathai became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A rover powers down
passages.text: The rover's battery output had fallen below the level engineers considered safe for driving. ______ mission controllers put it into a low-power sleep mode until the Martian spring brought stronger sunlight to its solar panels.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Roads in the mountains
passages.text: Stretching for tens of thousands of kilometers across the Andes______ the Inca road system linked an empire that had no wheeled vehicles and no horses.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A striking feature
passages.text: The most ______ feature of the new library is its glass reading room, which juts out over the river and is the first thing visitors notice as they cross the bridge into town.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A narrow program
passages.text: Critics called the festival's programming ______: nearly every film had been made in the host city, and only one of the forty screenings came from outside the region.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: One giant tree
passages.text: In central Utah grows a stand of about 47,000 quaking aspen trunks known as Pando. Genetic tests show that every trunk is part of a single organism connected by one root system, making Pando one of the heaviest living things known. The stand, however, is no longer replacing its aging trunks. Deer and cattle eat the young shoots that sprout from the roots, and in areas where these animals can graze, few new trunks survive to replace the old ones.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Learning to dance
passages.text: Honeybees tell nestmates where to find food through a "waggle dance" whose angle and duration encode direction and distance. In one experiment, researchers raised colonies in which young bees could not watch older bees dance before dancing themselves. The first dances of these bees were more disordered than those of bees that had watched experienced dancers. With practice, their dances became more orderly, but their signals for distance remained less accurate throughout their lives. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seeds in storage
passages.text:
A seed bank tested how many seeds of one crop variety still germinated after ten years of storage at three temperatures.
Storage temperature | Seeds that germinated after 10 years
−18°C | 95%
4°C | 80%
20°C | 30%
The researchers concluded that seeds stored frozen kept nearly all their ability to germinate, while seeds kept at room temperature (about 20°C) lost most of it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: When Vesuvius erupted
passages.text: For centuries, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius that buried Pompeii was dated to August 24, 79 CE, based on copies of a letter by the Roman writer Pliny the Younger. Some archaeologists have argued that the eruption actually happened in the autumn, perhaps in October, and that the date in the surviving copies of the letter was miscopied.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Neanderthal art (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
For much of the twentieth century, many researchers held that Neanderthals lacked the capacity for symbolic thought, pointing to the absence of clear Neanderthal art. Cave paintings, they argued, appeared only after modern humans arrived in Europe.
Text 2
In 2018, a team dated thin mineral crusts that had formed over red markings in three Spanish caves. The crusts, and therefore the markings beneath them, were at least 64,000 years old—about 20,000 years before modern humans are thought to have reached the region. If the dates hold up, the markings must have been made by Neanderthals.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Ramanujan
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Srinivasa Ramanujan was born in India in 1887.
• He had little formal training in advanced mathematics and largely taught himself.
• In 1913, he sent pages of his results to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy.
• Hardy invited him to Cambridge, where they worked together for several years.
• In 1918, Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Quieter buses
passages.text: The city's new electric buses are quieter and produce no exhaust on the street. ______ each one costs nearly twice as much to buy as the diesel bus it replaces, a difference the city expects to recover only gradually through lower fuel and repair costs.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A small effect
passages.text: Despite predictions that the fare increase would drive riders away, the change had little ______ on the number of people using the subway each weekday.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Exhibit
passages.text: The museum's new exhibit focuses on three everyday objects whose inventors are largely ______ the folding ladder, the safety pin, and the paper clip.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Festival lineup
passages.text: This year's festival lineup includes the Ramos Quartet, a string ensemble from ______ Aiko Tanaka, a percussionist from Osaka; and the Northfield Choir, which will close the final evening.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Blue pigment
passages.text: The pigment—made by grinding a blue mineral that was carried by traders from distant ______ was so costly that painters often reserved it for the robes of a painting's most important figures.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Expedition water
passages.text: The expedition's success depended on a single ______ fresh water, which had to be carried in from a spring two days' walk away.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bacteria experiment
passages.text: Because the samples had been contaminated during ______ the team discarded them and repeated the entire experiment with fresh cultures.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Reef survey
passages.text: Most of the coral colonies in the survey area had recovered within five years of the bleaching event. The colonies on the reef's outer ______ showed almost no recovery, possibly because warmer currents reached them first.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shared bikes
passages.text:
A city analyst compared daily trips on its shared-bike system before and after it added 40 docking stations in outlying neighborhoods.
Average weekday trips: central stations 5,200 before and 5,150 after; outlying stations 300 before and 1,450 after.
Average weekend trips: central stations 3,100 before and 3,050 after; outlying stations 250 before and 1,900 after.
The analyst concluded that the new stations increased total ridership rather than merely shifting riders away from central stations, and that the increase was proportionally larger on weekends.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seed banks
passages.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores duplicate samples of seeds held by gene banks around the world. In 2015, researchers at a gene bank in Syria, whose collection had been damaged by war, ______ the first withdrawal from the vault, using the duplicates to rebuild their collection in Lebanon and Morocco.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Measuring a coastline
passages.text: In the mid-twentieth century, the scientist Lewis Fry Richardson noticed that the measured length of a coastline grows as the measuring stick gets shorter, because a shorter stick follows smaller inlets and bends. ______ the coastline of Britain measured with a 200-kilometer stick is about 2,400 kilometers long, but measured with a 50-kilometer stick it is about 3,400 kilometers.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a dye
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1856, 18-year-old William Perkin tried to make quinine, a malaria drug, from coal tar.
- The attempt failed, but it produced a purple substance.
- Perkin found the substance could dye silk and did not fade in sunlight or washing.
- He named it mauveine and opened a factory to produce it.
- Before mauveine, purple dyes came from sources such as sea snails and were very expensive.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A cautious endorsement
passages.text: The panel's report on the new water filter was carefully ______: it confirmed that the device removed lead in laboratory tests but declined to say whether it would perform as well in older homes, where pipes shed metal particles unevenly.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Glassfrogs at rest
passages.text: Glassfrogs have transparent skin and muscle, yet their red blood would ordinarily make them easy for predators to spot. Researchers found that when a glassfrog sleeps, it removes nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells from circulation and packs them into its liver, whose reflective surface hides them; when the frog wakes and becomes active, the cells return to its bloodstream. Remarkably, the packed cells do not form the clots that such dense crowding of blood cells causes in most animals. This finding has drawn interest from medical researchers, since it suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Noise and nests
passages.text: Ecologist Clinton Francis compared nesting birds near natural-gas wells fitted with noisy compressors and near quiet wells in New Mexico. Western scrub jays, which eat other birds' eggs, avoided the noisy sites. As a result, some species, such as black-chinned hummingbirds, nested more successfully near the noisy compressors than near quiet wells. Francis argues that the effects of noise on a bird species cannot be predicted from how well that species tolerates noise alone.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two views of the Antikythera mechanism
passages.text:
Text 1
The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze gearwork recovered from a shipwreck dated to the first century BCE, predicted eclipses and tracked the positions of the Sun and Moon. Some historians argue that its precision implies a long tradition of similar devices, now lost, since a machine this refined is unlikely to have been the first of its kind.

Text 2
Other historians note that the mechanism's gear teeth were cut by hand and are slightly irregular, and that some of its predictions would have drifted noticeably within a few years. To these historians, the imperfections suggest a workshop still solving basic problems of construction rather than one refining a mature craft. Yet they grant that metal objects were routinely melted down for reuse, so the absence of other such devices proves little.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A novelist's revision
passages.text: When the novelist Kaya Ostrander revised her first book for a new edition twenty years after it appeared, readers expected her to modernize its dated slang. Instead, she left every line of dialogue untouched and rewrote only the narrator's commentary, removing the knowing asides that had once explained the characters to the reader. The characters' speech, she wrote in a preface, was "a record of how people sounded"; the narrator's explanations were "a record only of how much I distrusted my readers."
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Coincidence in fiction
passages.text: Although critics praised the novelist's dialogue as true to life, they found her plots ______: each one resolved its central conflict through a coincidence that nothing earlier in the story had prepared the reader to accept.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lanes and riders
passages.text: In a survey of 30 cities, those with the most kilometers of protected bike lanes also had the highest shares of commuters who travel by bicycle. Some planners conclude that building protected lanes leads more people to cycle. Others argue that the relationship runs the other way: cities where many residents already cycled were simply more likely to build lanes.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Drought trials
passages.text:
An agronomist grew four wheat varieties under normal watering and under drought conditions and recorded each variety's yield, in bushels per acre.
Variety A: 52 normal, 20 drought
Variety B: 48 normal, 31 drought
Variety C: 55 normal, 24 drought
Variety D: 40 normal, 29 drought
The agronomist claims that the variety best suited to normal watering is not the variety best suited to drought.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Newton's mirror
passages.text: Early telescopes used lenses, which bend different colors of light by slightly different amounts and so surround images with colored fringes. Isaac Newton's reflecting telescope of 1668 avoided this problem by gathering light with a curved mirror instead. ______ the mirrors of the period were made of speculum metal, which tarnished quickly and reflected only about two-thirds of the light that struck it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Self-taught mathematicians
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Sophie Germain (1776–1831) of France was barred from university study because she was a woman.
- She studied mathematics from her father's books and wrote to Carl Friedrich Gauss under a male pen name.
- Mary Somerville (1780–1872) of Scotland received little formal schooling.
- She first encountered algebra in a puzzle printed in a fashion magazine and then studied it on her own.
- Germain did research in number theory; Somerville became known for explaining astronomy to general readers.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shade and sun
passages.text: In many plant species, individuals that grow in shade produce larger but thinner leaves than individuals of the same species grown in full sun. In a greenhouse study, seedlings of a forest herb raised in shade and then moved into full sun suffered more leaf damage than seedlings raised in full sun from the start, even though the two groups had the same total leaf area when the move occurred. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Letters and meaning
passages.text:
Text 1
Some literary scholars hold that a novel's meaning is fixed by what its author intended. On this view, when readers disagree about a passage, an author's letters or notebooks should settle the dispute, since they offer direct evidence of intention.

Text 2
Other scholars argue that readers encounter only the published book and that interpretation must therefore rest on the text itself. These scholars do grant that an author's letters can be useful in one respect: they can show what a word meant to writers and readers at the time the book was written, a meaning that may since have changed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Where the water went
passages.text:
A city's total water use fell from 120 million to 96 million liters per day between 2010 and 2020. The table shows average daily use, in millions of liters, by category.
Lawn and garden watering: 40 in 2010, 22 in 2020
Indoor household use: 55 in 2010, 50 in 2020
Commercial and other use: 25 in 2010, 24 in 2020
A city analyst claims that most of the decline in total water use came from reduced lawn and garden watering.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Second thoughts
passages.text: When the photographer's first exhibition opened, many critics dismissed the prints as mere technical exercises, unworthy of comparison with painting. ______ several of those same critics praised her compositions a decade later, once photography had gained acceptance as an art, suggesting that their original objection had been to the medium rather than to her work.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A dissenting reading
passages.text: For decades, historians described the town's 1890s building boom as the work of outside investors who arrived with the railroad. Historian Imani Torres questions this account. Examining property records, she found that more than half of the new buildings were financed by local families who had lived in the town since before the railroad came. Torres does not deny that the railroad mattered; rather, she argues that it gave existing residents a reason to invest in their own town.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Three venues
passages.text: This year's festival used three ______ a converted grain mill, which hosted the film screenings; a riverside tent, which held the evening concerts; and the town library, which housed the poetry readings.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a bridge
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State opened in July 1940.
- Its deck was unusually narrow and shallow for its length.
- In November 1940, a steady wind of about 40 miles per hour set the deck twisting.
- The twisting grew until the main span collapsed; no people were killed.
- After the collapse, testing scale models in wind tunnels became a standard step in designing long suspension bridges.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A reluctant witness
passages.text: In the novel's final chapter, the narrator, who has spent the book insisting that she saw nothing on the night of the fire, finally admits to having noticed a light in the barn. Her confession is ______: she offers it only after the other characters have already pieced together what happened, so it changes nothing about the outcome.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bird song in cities
passages.text: Researchers recording great tits in European cities found that urban males sang at higher minimum pitches than males of the same species in nearby forests. Low-pitched city noise from traffic overlaps with the lower part of the birds' songs. Some researchers have proposed that singing higher helps urban males be heard over the noise. Others have suggested that the difference reflects something else about city birds, such as their smaller body size. The finding that would most directly support the first explanation is one showing that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Library visits
passages.text:
A town librarian compared monthly in-person visits before and after the library extended its weekday hours from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m.
Before the change: 4,200 visits per month, 600 of them after 5 p.m.
After the change: 4,900 visits per month, 1,400 of them after 5 p.m.
The librarian claims that the longer hours attracted new evening visits rather than simply shifting existing visitors from earlier in the day.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two kinds of evidence
passages.text:
Text 1
For much of the twentieth century, historians of medieval villages relied mainly on written records such as tax rolls and court documents. These sources, one historian argues, give the most reliable picture of village life, because they record names, amounts, and dates.

Text 2
Archaeologist Rhea Moss points out that written records were produced by officials and describe mainly what officials cared about: taxes owed and crimes punished. Excavations of village houses, she notes, reveal what people actually ate, how they built their homes, and which goods they traded—matters the records rarely mention. Moss does not dismiss written sources, but she argues that neither kind of evidence is complete without the other.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Glass sponges
passages.text: Venus's flower basket, a deep-sea sponge, builds its skeleton from fine strands of silica glass. Engineers studying the skeleton found that its lattice of crossing strands, reinforced by diagonal struts, resists bending far better than a lattice of the same mass without the diagonals. The researchers suggested that the sponge's design could guide the construction of lightweight towers and bridges.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A coded diary
passages.text: Historians long assumed that the small diary, written in an unfamiliar shorthand, contained only household accounts. When a graduate student finally deciphered the shorthand in 2019, she discovered ______ entries describing the writer's work as a messenger during the war.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Measuring a glacier
passages.text: To measure how fast the glacier was moving, the team drove stakes into the ice in a straight line across its ______ year later, they surveyed the stakes again and found that the line had bent into a curve, with the stakes near the center having moved farthest.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A busy street
passages.text: The number of cyclists using the new bridge, according to counts taken by the city's transportation office over the first three months, ______ steadily each week.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A careful conclusion
passages.text: Early studies suggested that a certain herb reduced the length of common colds. ______ later studies with larger groups and with participants who did not know whether they were taking the herb or a placebo found no difference in how long colds lasted.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a canal
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Erie Canal opened in New York State in 1825.
- It connected the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo.
- Before the canal, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City could cost about $100.
- After the canal opened, the cost fell to roughly $10 per ton.
- New York City soon became the busiest port in the United States.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Railroad time
passages.text: Before the 1880s, most towns in the United States set their clocks by the sun, so noon in one town might fall several minutes before noon in a town a short distance to the west. A historian argues that railroads, which needed consistent schedules across long distances, were chiefly responsible for ending this practice.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Festival founders
passages.text: The festival's founders—two retired teachers, a baker, and a local ______ expected it to draw visitors from outside the county, yet last year it attracted more than twenty thousand people.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The surveyor's notebooks
passages.text: The surveyor's field notebooks, recovered from a farmhouse attic in 1987 and now held in the state library's special collections, ______ the earliest detailed description of the valley's river system.
passages.author: ai:claude
