passages.title: Lichen survey
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Many lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide, an air pollutant.
- In a 2015 survey, volunteers counted lichen species on trees across a city.
- Sites far from major roads had an average of 11 lichen species; sites near major roads had an average of 4.
- The survey did not measure sulfur dioxide directly.
- Lichens can also be affected by tree bark acidity and by shade.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An inevitable treaty?
passages.text: Although the historian's account of the treaty negotiations is meticulously documented, her conclusion that the agreement was inevitable seems ______, since several of the letters she herself cites show delegates on the verge of abandoning the talks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Spines on demand
passages.text: Some water fleas grow protective spines only when they detect chemicals released by their predator, a midge larva. The spines lower a flea's risk of being eaten but slow its reproduction. Researchers collected fleas from a lake where midge larvae had been absent for several decades and exposed them to midge chemicals in the laboratory. These fleas grew spines just as readily as fleas taken from lakes where midges were common, which suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shade trees
passages.text:
A city planted trees along some streets in 2019 to reduce summer heat. A researcher compared average midday street-surface temperatures in July.
Streets with new trees: 41°C in 2018; 38°C in 2023.
Streets without new trees: 40°C in 2018; 40°C in 2023.
The researcher concludes that the trees, rather than a citywide change in weather, most likely explain the cooling on the planted streets.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Dating a map
passages.text: The museum's oldest map was long thought to date from the early ______ recent analysis of its paper, however, suggests that it was drawn more than a century later.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Saturn's rings
passages.text: For two centuries after their discovery, many astronomers assumed that Saturn's rings were solid sheets of material. In the 1850s, the physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed mathematically that a solid ring of that size would be torn apart by Saturn's gravity. ______ he argued, the rings must consist of countless separate particles, each orbiting the planet on its own.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Tree rings and a shipwreck
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Divers found the wreck of a wooden ship in the Baltic Sea.
- Radiocarbon dating of the wood gave a possible range of about 150 years.
- Each year's weather affects how wide a tree's growth ring is, so a sequence of rings forms a pattern unique to those years.
- Researchers matched the ring pattern in the ship's oak planks to a regional record of tree-ring widths.
- The match showed that the trees were cut down in the winter of 1611-1612.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A mixed review
passages.text: The critic's praise for the new film was ______: although she admired its cinematography, she devoted most of her review to faulting the script, the pacing, and the lead performance.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Marigolds and nematodes
passages.text: Farmers have long noticed that tomato plants grown beside marigolds suffer less damage from root-knot nematodes, tiny worms that attack roots. One explanation is that marigold roots release a compound that is toxic to the nematodes; another is that marigolds encourage the growth of soil fungi that prey on nematodes. To test these ideas, researchers sterilized a batch of soil, killing any fungi, and then added equal numbers of nematodes to sterilized and unsterilized pots, each containing a tomato plant beside a marigold. Nematode numbers ended up just as low in the sterilized pots as in the unsterilized ones, and both were far lower than in comparison pots without marigolds, which suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A reading app
passages.text:
A school district gave a reading app to some students in grades 4 and 5 and compared their gains on a spring reading test with the gains of students who did not use the app.
Students who began the year below grade level: app users gained 14 points; nonusers gained 6 points.
Students who began the year at grade level: app users gained 9 points; nonusers gained 5 points.
A district analyst concludes that the app benefited students who began below grade level more than it benefited students who began at grade level.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Why a dialect fades
passages.text:
Text 1
In the valleys of one mountain region, younger residents use far fewer of the region's traditional dialect features than their grandparents do. A linguist attributes the change to television, arguing that decades of exposure to broadcast speech have pulled local speakers toward a national standard.

Text 2
Sociolinguist Mara Vint interviewed residents of the same region who reported watching similar amounts of television. Those who had spent several years working in distant cities had dropped most dialect features, while those who had always lived in the valleys still used them heavily. Vint argues that face-to-face contact with speakers of other varieties, not broadcast speech, reshapes how people talk.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The order slip
passages.text: Mrs. Avery had kept the bookshop for thirty years and prided herself on finding any book a customer could name. When a young man came in asking for a novel she had never heard of, she smiled and promised to order it. After he left, she wrote the title on a slip of paper, studied it for a long moment, and then tucked it into the drawer where she kept the letters she did not intend to answer.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Newton's telescope
passages.text: Early telescopes surrounded their images with fringes of false color, because their glass lenses bent different colors of light by different amounts. Isaac Newton concluded, wrongly as it turned out, that no arrangement of lenses could ever remove this flaw. ______ he built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror, which reflects all colors equally.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A careful report
passages.text: The review committee's report on the proposed stadium was notably ______: it listed the plan's costs and benefits in detail but declined to say whether the city should go ahead with the project.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Roman harbor concrete
passages.text: Some concrete structures built in Roman harbors have survived roughly two thousand years of exposure to seawater, while modern concrete in similar conditions can crumble within decades. The difference long puzzled engineers. Analyzing samples from Roman harbors, researchers found that seawater seeping through the concrete reacted with volcanic ash in the original mix, growing new mineral crystals that filled cracks and strengthened the material over time.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Crows and masks
passages.text: In a long-term study, researchers wearing a distinctive mask briefly captured and released several wild crows on a college campus. For years afterward, crows on the campus scolded and dived at anyone wearing that mask but ignored people wearing a different, neutral mask. The researchers hypothesized that crows learn to recognize dangerous people not only from their own experience but also by observing other crows.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Birds along trails
passages.text: An ecologist surveyed bird species in a forest by having observers walk the forest's trails at dawn and record every species they heard singing. Observers recorded more species near trailheads than deep in the forest. However, because the observers walked only along trails and could hear birds only within about fifty meters, the ecologist cautioned that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A shorter week
passages.text:
Text 1
An economist studying companies that adopted a four-day workweek found that their output per employee rose by an average of 8 percent in the following year. She argues that a shorter week could raise productivity across the economy.

Text 2
A labor researcher notes that the companies in the study chose to try the four-day week, and many were firms whose managers already believed their work could be done in less time. Results from such firms, he argues, may say little about how a shorter week would work at companies that would not have chosen it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two writers
passages.text: Having spent a decade comparing the handwriting, ink, and paper of the letters, ______ that they were written by two different people rather than one.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Load ratings
passages.text: The new bridge across the river was designed to carry far heavier traffic than the one it replaced. ______ engineers rated it to support trucks weighing up to forty tons, about twice the limit on the old bridge.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Early results
passages.text: Although the new treatment's early results were promising, the researchers were careful not to ______ them, noting that the trial had included only forty patients and had lasted just six weeks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The ferry
passages.text: The old ferry had crossed the river twice a day for sixty years. Most people in town no longer noticed its horn. When the county announced that a new bridge would replace it, people who had not ridden the ferry in decades wrote letters to the newspaper demanding that it be saved.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Desert seeds
passages.text: The seeds of a certain desert plant contain a chemical that prevents them from germinating. Heavy rainfall washes the chemical out of the seed coat, but a light shower does not. In laboratory tests, seeds soaked in water for a few minutes rarely germinated, while seeds soaked for several hours germinated readily. This mechanism likely benefits the plant because ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two cities
passages.text:
A demographer compared the populations of two cities.
City A: 50,000 residents in 2000; 80,000 residents in 2020.
City B: 120,000 residents in 2000; 150,000 residents in 2020.
The demographer claims that although the two cities gained the same number of residents, city A grew much faster in percentage terms.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A popular gallery
passages.text: The museum's newest gallery, which opened in ______ already drawn more visitors than any other exhibit in the building's history.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A summer tradition
passages.text: The tradition of building sandcastles on the town's beach each July, which began more than a century ago as a contest for local children, ______ to draw thousands of visitors every summer.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An unexplored cave
passages.text: Early accounts described the cave as a single, modest chamber. Later surveys found it to be far larger, with dozens of connected passages stretching for kilometers. ______ the original explorers, working by candlelight, had seen only the entrance hall.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Axolotl regrowth
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The axolotl is a salamander native to lakes near Mexico City.
- Unlike most salamanders, it keeps its gills and lives in water as an adult.
- It can regrow lost limbs, including bone and muscle.
- Researchers have found that axolotls regrow limbs more slowly as they age.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rural and urban survey
passages.text: In a state survey, 200 rural residents and 800 urban residents were asked whether they had used a public library in the past month. Of the rural residents, 30 percent said yes; of the urban residents, 20 percent said yes. A reporter claims that more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library, even though a smaller percentage of urban residents had.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two great rivers
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river.
- The Congo River carries the second-largest volume of water.
- Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
- The Amazon is roughly 6,400 kilometers long; the Congo is roughly 4,700 kilometers long.
- Parts of the Congo are more than 200 meters deep.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An austere poet
passages.text: Critics often call the poet's late work austere, but the label is somewhat ______: although her diction in these poems is indeed spare, the poems themselves are dense with allusions to scripture, folk song, and her own earlier work, and they reward patient rereading.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Perches and shrubs
passages.text: Birds deposit most of the seeds they eat beneath the places where they perch, so plants whose seeds are spread by birds often grow in clusters around trees and fences. In a restored grassland, ecologists installed artificial perches in some plots and left others without perches. After three years, shrubs spread by birds had become established in the perch plots at five times their density in the other plots, while plants spread by wind showed no difference between the two kinds of plots. These results suggest that, in this grassland, the establishment of bird-spread shrubs had been limited mainly by ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Printing and spelling
passages.text:
Text 1
Many historians have credited the printing press with rapidly standardizing English spelling. Once texts could be reproduced in thousands of identical copies, they argue, printers quickly settled on uniform spellings that readers then absorbed.

Text 2
Historian Ada Kwan examined books printed in London between 1500 and 1650 and found that spellings varied widely, even among books from the same print shop and sometimes on the same page. Kwan does not deny that printing contributed to standard spelling, but she argues that uniform spelling took hold only gradually, after dictionaries and schoolbooks spread fixed forms in the late 1600s and 1700s.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Fertilizer in dry years
passages.text:
Researchers tested a new fertilizer on wheat in a dry year and a wet year.
Dry year: 2.0 tonnes per hectare without fertilizer; 2.6 with fertilizer.
Wet year: 3.5 tonnes per hectare without fertilizer; 3.8 with fertilizer.
The researchers claim that the fertilizer's benefit was greater in the dry year, whether measured in tonnes or as a percentage of the unfertilized yield.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Discovered or invented?
passages.text: Philosophers have long debated whether moral principles are discovered, like facts about the physical world, or invented, like the rules of a game. Defenders of discovery often point to the striking similarities among the moral codes of societies that had no contact with one another. Yet such similarities are also what the invention view would predict if those codes arose as solutions to problems that every society faces, such as dividing food and settling disputes. The similarities alone, then, cannot settle the question.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Expedition supplies
passages.text: To keep their sleds light on the long crossing of the ice sheet, the team carried only three ______ water, a compass, and a satellite radio.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A costly flaw
passages.text: If the engineers ______ the flaw in the bridge's design sooner, the structure would not have needed the costly repairs that closed it for most of last year.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Jevons's coal question
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons studied Britain's use of coal.
- Steam engines had become far more efficient, using less coal for the same work.
- Jevons observed that Britain's total coal use had risen rather than fallen.
- More efficient engines made coal-powered work cheaper.
- Cheaper coal-powered work led people to use coal for many more tasks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A change in tone
passages.text: The chemist's early papers were notably ______, hedging nearly every conclusion and noting the limits of each experiment, but her later work stated its claims with striking confidence.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Words for parents
passages.text: In many unrelated languages, the word for "mother" begins with an m sound. One explanation is that m is among the first sounds infants make, since it requires only closing the lips while using the voice, and parents may have taken an infant's early babbling as a name for the mother. If this explanation is correct, words for "father" in many unrelated languages would also be expected to ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Minimum wage studies
passages.text: Economists have often described raising the minimum wage as a tradeoff: workers who keep their jobs earn more, but fewer jobs are available. A growing number of studies, however, have found little or no loss of employment after moderate increases. These findings do not show that every increase is harmless. Most of the studies examined raises of modest size, and the effects of much larger increases remain uncertain.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rainfall in two regions
passages.text:
Average yearly rainfall, in millimeters, in two regions:
Region X: 820 in 2010; 760 in 2015; 700 in 2020.
Region Y: 640 in 2010; 650 in 2015; 600 in 2020.
A researcher claims that rainfall declined steadily in Region X over this period, whereas rainfall in Region Y did not decline consistently.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A reopened archive
passages.text: The city's archive had been closed to the public for ______ researchers were finally admitted in 2019, after a team of librarians had finished cataloging its contents.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An abrupt ending
passages.text: Critics have called the novel's ending abrupt. ______ the final chapter is only two pages long and leaves several subplots unresolved. Yet the abruptness seems deliberate: the narrator, who has controlled every detail of the story, finally loses control of it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Animal tools
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Sea otters float on their backs and use rocks to crack open shellfish.
- New Caledonian crows shape twigs and leaves into hooks for pulling insects from holes.
- Some octopuses carry coconut shell halves and assemble them into shelters.
- Sea otters are mammals, crows are birds, and octopuses are mollusks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A late style
passages.text: The novelist's prose is usually praised as lucid, but in her final book the sentences grow deliberately ______, folding clause into clause until readers must go back to the beginning to follow them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Thinner bowls
passages.text: At an ancient village site, bowls made over a span of two centuries became steadily thinner-walled and more uniform in shape. Researchers had attributed the change to the arrival of the potter's wheel, which appears at the site at the start of that period. However, at a nearby village where potters never adopted the wheel, bowls from the same two centuries show the same gradual thinning. This suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Study time and scores
passages.text:
A school compared students' weekly study time with their average scores on a final exam.
0-2 hours per week: average score 62
3-5 hours per week: average score 74
6-8 hours per week: average score 79
9-11 hours per week: average score 81
A teacher concludes that students who studied more tended to score higher, but that each additional block of study time was associated with a smaller gain.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Egg shapes
passages.text: Some birds lay eggs that are sharply pointed at one end. A long-standing explanation held that the shape keeps eggs from rolling off cliff ledges. Yet many pointed eggs are laid by birds that nest on flat ground. A study of eggs from more than 1,400 bird species found instead that egg shape is linked to flying ability: strong fliers tend to lay more elongated eggs, perhaps because a streamlined body limits how wide an egg can be.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A traveling fungus
passages.text: After years of searching, the researchers finally identified the cause of the trees' ______ a fungus that had been carried into the region on imported timber.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Willows on the bank
passages.text: Along the eroding riverbank, where volunteers planted cuttings last spring, ______ several species of willow that root easily and help hold the soil in place.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Sunny-day flooding
passages.text: Many coastal cities now experience what planners call "sunny-day flooding." ______ streets near the shore fill with seawater during especially high tides, even when no rain has fallen.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A bold report
passages.text: Though the committee's final report was ______ in tone, avoiding dramatic language and acknowledging the arguments on every side, its recommendations were bold: it called for closing two aging schools and building a new one.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Warned about headaches
passages.text: In a study, volunteers were randomly assigned to take an inactive pill under one of two conditions. One group was told that the pill might cause headaches; the other group received the same pill without that warning. Volunteers who were warned reported headaches at about twice the rate of those who were not. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bike commuters
passages.text: In a city, 4 percent of the 200,000 workers commuted by bicycle in 2015. By 2023, the number of workers had grown to 300,000, and 6 percent of them commuted by bicycle. A transportation planner claims that the number of bicycle commuters more than doubled even though the share of workers who cycled rose by only half.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Medieval guilds
passages.text: Historians once portrayed medieval craft guilds mainly as monopolies that protected their members by blocking new techniques. Recent studies of guild records paint a more mixed picture. Some guilds did suppress innovations that threatened their members, but others funded apprenticeships that spread skills and set quality standards that allowed distant buyers to trust unfamiliar goods. Whether a guild helped or hindered economic growth, these studies suggest, depended less on guilds as such than on how each one was governed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Sensor drift
passages.text: Had the engineers ______ the sensor data more closely, they would have noticed the gradual drift in the readings weeks before the failure.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Red autumn leaves
passages.text:
Text 1
Why do some trees turn red in autumn rather than simply yellow? One botanist argues that the red pigments act as a sunscreen: as a leaf withdraws its nutrients before falling, the pigments shield it from sunlight damage, allowing the tree to recover more of those nutrients.

Text 2
Ecologists comparing tree species across regions found that trees with red autumn leaves are especially common where insects such as aphids, which lay their eggs on trees in autumn, are abundant. They propose that red coloring may advertise a tree's chemical defenses to these insects, discouraging them from laying eggs on it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An account of a strike
passages.text: Reviewers of the historian's new book on the 1912 mill strike have praised it as notably ______: she presents the demands of both the workers and the mill owners, quotes each side at length, and withholds her own judgment until the final chapter, where she argues that both sides misread the economic pressures they faced.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Do octopuses dream?
passages.text: Researchers observing octopuses in the lab noticed that sleeping animals sometimes cycled rapidly through skin color patterns while their eyes and arms twitched. Because these bouts resembled the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep of mammals, some commentators suggested that octopuses might dream. The researchers cautioned, however, that the color changes could simply reflect the nervous system replaying patterns the animals had used while awake, a process that need not involve any experience like dreaming. They proposed testing whether the patterns displayed during sleep matched those displayed during the day.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rent control
passages.text:
Text 1
Critics of rent control argue that it helps no one in the long run. By capping what landlords can charge, they say, rent control discourages owners from maintaining or supplying rental housing, so tenants ultimately face fewer and worse options.

Text 2
Economists studying a 1994 expansion of rent control in San Francisco compared buildings that became covered with similar buildings that did not. Tenants in covered buildings were significantly more likely to still be living at the same address years later. But owners of covered buildings reduced the number of rental units they offered by about 15 percent, often by converting apartments into condominiums.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Ana's hometown
passages.text: A student is writing about a novel whose narrator, Ana, returns to the river town where she grew up. The student claims that in the opening chapter Ana regards her hometown with both affection and impatience.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A find in the dunes
passages.text: The expedition's most valuable find, a set of bronze tools still bearing the marks of their ______ was uncovered on the last day of the dig, after a storm shifted the dunes.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A smaller trial
passages.text: The vaccine trial enrolled fewer participants than planned, which limited its ability to detect rare side effects. ______ the trial showed clearly that the vaccine reduced hospitalizations among the people who received it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A record span
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Akashi Kaikyō Bridge links the city of Kobe to Awaji Island in Japan.
- It opened in 1998.
- Its central span is 1,991 meters long.
- For more than two decades, that was the longest suspension-bridge span in the world.
- In 2022, the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey opened with a central span of 2,023 meters.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Late quartets
passages.text: Although the composer's late string quartets were at first dismissed as ______, later critics came to hear their abrupt shifts of mood and fragmentary forms as deliberate experiments rather than as signs of a declining talent that could no longer hold a piece together.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seedlings and distance
passages.text:
The Janzen-Connell hypothesis holds that tree seedlings growing close to a parent tree survive less often than those farther away, because pests that specialize on that species gather near the parent. A biologist tracked seedlings of two tree species in a tropical forest and concluded that the pattern holds for species A but not for species B.
Percentage of seedlings surviving after one year
Distance from parent tree | Species A | Species B
0-5 meters | 12% | 30%
5-20 meters | 25% | 31%
more than 20 meters | 41% | 29%
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Pottery from one riverbank
passages.text: Chemical analysis shows that the clay in a distinctive style of pottery, found at sites spread across a region some 300 kilometers wide, all came from a single riverbank deposit. Some archaeologists have treated the pottery's wide distribution as evidence that the communities at those sites shared a common culture with shared craft traditions. Because the clay came from one source, however, the distribution may instead indicate that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A team of specialists
passages.text: The members of the 1925 survey team included Ada Moreno, a ______ Lionel Park, a geologist; and Ruth Okafor, a photographer who later published the expedition's only surviving images.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Conflicting findings
passages.text: The two ______ findings contradicted each other: one reported that the drug lowered blood pressure, and the other found no effect at all.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Photography's early critics
passages.text: Many nineteenth-century critics dismissed photography as a mechanical process rather than an art. ______ the poet Charles Baudelaire wrote in 1859 that photography should be the "very humble servant" of the arts and sciences, not an art itself.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Waiting for a treat
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1960s and 1970s, psychologist Walter Mischel ran experiments at a Stanford University nursery school.
- Children could eat one treat right away or wait to receive two treats.
- Follow-up studies found that children who waited longer tended to have higher academic achievement years later.
- A 2018 study tested this link with a larger and more diverse sample of children.
- It found that the link was much weaker and was largely explained by differences in children's family backgrounds.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A winter crossing
passages.text: In the story, Teodor has crossed the frozen lake every winter for forty years, and the villagers treat his judgment about the ice as law. This year, however, he stops at the shore, tests the surface with his staff, and says nothing; the narrator observes that the silence of a man who has always been certain ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The waggle dance
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Honeybees perform a "waggle dance" that tells nestmates the direction and distance of a food source.
- The dance was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by Karl von Frisch.
- Researchers later prevented some colonies from reading dance directions.
- In some seasons, those colonies gathered about as much food as colonies that could read the dances.
- In other seasons, colonies that could read the dances gathered noticeably more food.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Cathedrals by committee
passages.text: In arguing that the medieval cathedral was less the monument to a single vision than an accretion of compromises among bishops, guilds, and successive master builders, the historian does not ______ the achievement of those who built it; rather, she relocates it, crediting collective negotiation with what earlier accounts had ascribed to individual genius.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Inventors and cities
passages.text: Economists have long observed that cities produce more patents per resident than rural areas do, and many have attributed the difference to the density of face-to-face contact among inventors. Yet the pattern admits another explanation: unusually inventive people may simply move to cities, bringing their productivity with them. To separate these possibilities, researchers followed individual inventors who relocated and found that the same people patented more after moving into larger clusters of inventors in their field, a result that the sorting explanation alone cannot accommodate.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Translating what is left open
passages.text: Translators of classical Chinese poetry face a peculiar difficulty. The originals often leave grammatical subject, tense, and number unstated, so that a line may describe one traveler or many, an event now or long past. English, which demands such choices, forces the translator to settle what the poem leaves open. Some translators accept this as an unavoidable loss; others have experimented with fragmentary English that preserves the openness at the cost of fluency. Neither approach, the critic argues, escapes the problem, for one sacrifices the poem's ambiguity and the other its ease, which is no less a part of its meaning.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Hope
passages.text:
The following text is from Emily Dickinson's poem "'Hope' is the thing with feathers," written around 1861.
"Hope" is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -
And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -
I've heard it in the chillest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of me.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: E-book loans
passages.text:
A county library system reported the number of e-books it loaned each year.
2017: 40,000
2018: 44,000
2019: 48,000
2020: 75,000
2021: 82,000
A researcher claims that the jump in e-book loans after 2019 was not simply a continuation of the system's earlier trend.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Whale songs
passages.text: Having analyzed thousands of hours of underwater recordings collected over a decade, ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bridge from a window
passages.text: By the time the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its chief engineer, Washington Roebling, ______ construction for more than a decade from a room overlooking the East River, having been disabled by decompression sickness he developed while working in the bridge's underwater foundations.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Short sentences
passages.text: Some reviewers have called the novelist's prose ______, but the charge mistakes economy for poverty: her sentences are short not because she lacks resources but because every word in them has been weighed and the unnecessary ones discarded.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Plants that stop flinching
passages.text: The leaves of Mimosa pudica fold up when the plant is disturbed, a response thought to protect it from being eaten. In one experiment, researchers repeatedly dropped potted Mimosa plants a short distance onto a padded surface. At first the plants folded their leaves after each drop, but after many drops most plants stopped folding. When the same plants were then shaken, a disturbance they had not experienced before, they folded their leaves at once. This result suggests that the plants' failure to fold after repeated drops was not simply ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The stability of print
passages.text:
Text 1
In an influential study, historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that the printing press transformed European learning by making texts fixed. Once a work was printed, she contended, hundreds of identical copies could circulate, so that scholars in different cities could be confident they were reading the same words.

Text 2
Historian Adrian Johns points out that early printed books were often anything but reliable. Printers pirated one another's editions, introduced errors, and sometimes altered texts to suit buyers. Readers trusted a printed book, Johns argues, only when they trusted the people and institutions behind it, such as reputable printers, licensing systems, and learned societies, and that trust took generations to build.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Parks and birds
passages.text:
An ecologist surveyed bird species in five city parks.
Park | Area (hectares) | Bird species recorded
P | 2 | 14
Q | 5 | 22
R | 9 | 19
S | 12 | 31
T | 20 | 38
The ecologist concluded that although larger parks generally had more bird species, park area alone did not determine the number of species recorded.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Small area, many species
passages.text: Coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean ______ they support roughly a quarter of all known marine species.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A report on transit
passages.text: After two years of study, the city's transit commission released ______ final report, which recommended extending light-rail service to the airport.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bike lanes on Main Street
passages.text: When the city built protected bike lanes on Main Street, planners predicted that many residents who had been afraid to ride in traffic would begin commuting by bicycle. ______ bicycle traffic on the street tripled within a year, while car traffic barely changed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Words for blue
passages.text:
Text 1
Some scholars have argued that the language a person speaks determines what that person can perceive: if a language lacks separate words for two colors, its speakers cannot truly see them as different.

Text 2
Russian has two basic words for blue: goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker ones. In one experiment, Russian speakers told apart two blues faster when the blues fell on opposite sides of that boundary than when both fell on the same side; English speakers, who use one basic word for both, showed no such difference. But the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they performed a verbal task, such as silently repeating a string of digits, at the same time, while a nonverbal task did not remove it. Language, the researchers concluded, can influence perception, but only while words are actively being used.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Plain houses
passages.text: Early reviewers dismissed the architect's houses as ______, but she regarded their plainness as a discipline: by refusing ornament, she forced visitors to notice proportion and the movement of light through each room.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Exact terms
passages.text: To many of her students, the professor's insistence on exact terminology seemed merely ______; only years later did they recognize it as the habit that had made their own arguments clear.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A song rebuilt
passages.text: Young male zebra finches learn their songs by copying adult tutors, and males raised without any tutor develop songs that sound abnormal. In one experiment, researchers founded a colony with such untutored males. Their sons copied the abnormal songs, but across several generations, as each new group of young males learned from the previous one, the colony's songs changed gradually until they came to resemble the songs of wild zebra finches. This result suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Music and reasoning
passages.text:
Text 1
In 1993, researchers reported that college students who listened to a Mozart sonata for ten minutes scored higher on a spatial reasoning task than students who sat in silence. The finding was widely reported as evidence that classical music makes listeners smarter.

Text 2
Later studies found that the improvement was small and lasted only minutes. In one study, students who listened to an audio story they enjoyed did as well on the spatial task as students who listened to Mozart, but only if they preferred the story to the music. The researchers concluded that the improvement reflects a listener's mood and alertness rather than anything special about Mozart's music.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Changeable skin
passages.text: ______ octopuses and cuttlefish can change not only the color but also the texture of their skin, raising small bumps that help them blend in with rocks and seaweed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A long collection
passages.text: Since its founding in 1850, the natural history society ______ more than ten thousand specimens of insects, many of them gathered by amateur members.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Galileo's moons
passages.text: Many of Galileo's contemporaries doubted that a telescope's images could be trusted, since the lenses of the time blurred and colored what they showed. ______ Galileo's 1610 observations of four moons orbiting Jupiter were soon confirmed by other astronomers using their own instruments.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A shrinking lake
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Lake Chad lies where Chad, Cameroon, Niger, and Nigeria meet.
- It is a shallow lake that has long been an important source of water and fish for the region.
- Since the 1960s, the lake has shrunk by about 90 percent.
- Repeated droughts have reduced the water flowing into the lake.
- Water has also been diverted from rivers that feed the lake to irrigate farmland.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seeing the unseen
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Inge Lehmann was a Danish seismologist.
- In 1936, she analyzed records of earthquake waves and concluded that Earth has a solid inner core.
- Marie Tharp was an American geologist and mapmaker.
- In the 1950s, she used measurements of ocean depth to map a rift valley running along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
- Neither scientist directly observed the structure she identified.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Broad terms
passages.text: Some historians have criticized the treaty's language as ______, but its drafters chose broad terms deliberately, so that later governments could apply the agreement to circumstances that no one at the negotiating table could foresee.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A partner in the hunt
passages.text: In parts of Mozambique, Yao honey hunters seek out wild bees' nests with the help of the greater honeyguide, a bird that leads people to nests and then eats the wax left behind after the hunters remove the honey. Hunters attract honeyguides with a special call, a trill followed by a grunt. When researchers played recordings of this call, of other human sounds, and of the calls of another bird species, honeyguides were far more likely to begin guiding in response to the hunters' call. This finding suggests that the honeyguides ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Reef fish
passages.text:
A team counted fish at reef sites where fishing is banned and at nearby sites where fishing is allowed.
Site type | Fish counted per survey, 2015 | Fish counted per survey, 2022
Protected | 120 | 210
Fished | 80 | 110
The team claims that protected sites gained more fish not only in number but also in proportion to how many they started with.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Early photographers
passages.text: In the decades after photography was introduced in 1839, a number of early photographers ______ their chemical recipes secret, fearing that rivals would copy their methods.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Training a rescue dog
passages.text: Having practiced the search routine dozens of times in empty fields, ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A mixed result
passages.text: The trial's results were ______: they showed that the drug reduced symptoms in most patients, but they also showed that the benefit faded within a few weeks of starting treatment.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Knotted records
passages.text: Early European observers dismissed Inca khipus, bundles of knotted cords, as ______ records that only the person who tied them could interpret. In the twentieth century, however, researchers showed that many khipus record numbers using a consistent base-ten system that any trained reader could decode.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The Iceman
passages.text: When hikers found the frozen body of a man in the Alps in 1991, researchers estimated that he had died about 5,300 years earlier, and many first assumed that he had died of exposure while crossing the mountains. In 2001, however, an X-ray revealed a stone arrowhead lodged in his left shoulder, near an artery that it had torn. These findings suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A cave closed to save it
passages.text: The paintings of animals in France's Lascaux cave, made roughly 17,000 years ago, survived for millennia in darkness and stable air. After the cave opened to the public in 1948, the breath of more than a thousand visitors a day raised the humidity and the level of carbon dioxide inside, and colonies of algae and fungi began to spread across the walls. In 1963 the cave was closed to the public, and visitors today tour a detailed replica built nearby.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: What makes a planet
passages.text:
Text 1
In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that orbits the Sun, is massive enough to have pulled itself into a nearly round shape, and has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit of other objects. Pluto, which shares its region of space with many icy bodies, fails the last test and was reclassified as a dwarf planet.

Text 2
Some planetary scientists object that the clearing requirement judges a body by its surroundings rather than by its own nature. A world's shape, geology, and internal processes, they argue, are what matter to the scientists who study it, and by those standards Pluto, with its mountains of ice and its layered atmosphere, behaves very much like a planet.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A careful copy
passages.text: The replica built near the Lascaux cave reproduces even the smallest features of the ______ the cracks in the rock, the bulges in the walls, and the exact shades of the ancient pigments.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Spreading growth
passages.text: By the time officials closed the Lascaux cave in 1963, algae ______ across large areas of the painted walls.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Still called a planet
passages.text: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet. ______ many scientists, teachers, and members of the public continue to call it a planet.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A fast library
passages.text: Searching a library's card catalog once required walking between drawers of index cards. ______ a reader can now search an online catalog in seconds from anywhere with an internet connection.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: One of a kind
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The daguerreotype was one of the first practical photographic processes.
- It was announced in France in 1839.
- Each image was formed directly on a polished, silver-coated copper plate.
- The process produced no negative.
- As a result, each daguerreotype was a single, unique image that could not be reproduced from the original plate.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Hot water, cold water
passages.text: For centuries, people have reported that hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water, a claim now known as the Mpemba effect. The effect has proved ______: some careful experiments have appeared to reproduce it, while others, which controlled for evaporation and for how far the water cooled below its freezing point before ice formed, found no such difference.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Sleep without electricity
passages.text: A common view holds that people in industrial societies sleep less than humans did before electric lighting. To test this view, Gandhi Yetish and colleagues tracked sleep in three groups who live without electricity: the Hadza of Tanzania, the San of Namibia, and the Tsimane of Bolivia. The groups slept an average of 5.7 to 7.1 hours a night, amounts similar to or lower than those reported for many industrial populations. If these groups' sleep resembles that of humans before electric lighting, the findings suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Word frequency
passages.text:
In many languages, a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank: the second most common word appears about half as often as the most common, the third about a third as often, and so on. A linguist counted words in a sample of English text.
Rank 1: 60,200 occurrences
Rank 2: 30,500 occurrences
Rank 3: 19,800 occurrences
Rank 10: 6,100 occurrences
The linguist claims that the sample fits this pattern even for words well below the top three.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A limit on friendships
passages.text:
Text 1
Anthropologist Robin Dunbar observed that, among primates, species with a larger neocortex tend to live in larger groups. Extending this relationship to humans, he proposed that people can maintain only about 150 stable relationships, a figure that became known as Dunbar's number.

Text 2
In 2021, Patrik Lindenfors and colleagues reanalyzed primate data using several updated statistical methods. The estimates for humans that they obtained ranged from single digits to several hundred, depending on the method and data used. The researchers concluded that no specific figure can be derived from this approach.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Pillars before farms
passages.text: Archaeologists long held that monumental building began only after people settled in farming villages, which could supply the labor and food that large projects require. At Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, however, massive carved stone pillars, some more than five meters tall, were raised roughly 11,000 years ago, apparently by people who still hunted and gathered their food. Some researchers have since proposed that gathering to build such sites may have encouraged the shift to farming, rather than the reverse.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A language from children
passages.text: In Hawaii in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, plantation workers from many countries communicated in a pidgin, a makeshift language with variable word order and few consistent markers of tense. Many of their children, who heard this pidgin as they grew up, came to speak a language with fixed word order and regular markers of tense. The linguist Derek Bickerton took this as evidence that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A rare survivor
passages.text: Johannes Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz printed about 180 copies of the Bible in the ______ fewer than 50 of them are known to survive, and many of those are incomplete.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A contagious cancer
passages.text: Devil facial tumor disease, a cancer that spreads between Tasmanian devils when they bite one another's faces, ______ reduced the wild devil population by roughly 80 percent since it was first observed in 1996.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Small, dim, and long-lived
passages.text: Most stars in the Milky Way are red dwarfs, which are smaller and dimmer than the Sun. A planet warm enough for liquid water would have to orbit very close to such a star, where frequent stellar flares could strip away its atmosphere. ______ red dwarfs can shine steadily for hundreds of billions of years or more, giving any life that does arise far more time to develop than a Sun-like star would allow.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a nurse
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Mary Seacole was born in Jamaica in 1805.
- During the Crimean War, she asked the British War Office to send her to the front as a nurse.
- Her application was turned down.
- She traveled to Crimea at her own expense and opened the British Hotel near Balaclava in 1855.
- There she provided meals, supplies, and care to soldiers.
- She described her experiences in an 1857 autobiography.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A shaped journey
passages.text: Matsuo Bashō's The Narrow Road to the Deep North, which recounts a journey he made in 1689, has long been read as a travel diary. Yet the book is in places ______: a diary kept by Sora, the companion who walked beside him, shows that Bashō changed dates, rearranged stops, and described at least one episode that Sora never mentions.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Building an illusion
passages.text: Male great bowerbirds build an avenue of sticks and decorate the court at its entrance with stones, bones, and shells. Researchers found that the objects are arranged so that they get larger with distance from the avenue, which can make the court look shorter to a female standing inside. When the researchers reversed the arrangement, placing large objects close and small ones far away, the males restored the original size gradient within a few days. This finding suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Warmer nights
passages.text:
A student measured air temperatures at a downtown site and at a farm 20 kilometers away on the same summer day.
Afternoon: downtown 31.0°C, farm 30.2°C
Night: downtown 22.5°C, farm 19.1°C
The student claims that the city's warming effect was much stronger at night than during the afternoon.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Who built the walls
passages.text:
Text 1
In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, several European writers who visited Great Zimbabwe, a complex of massive stone walls in southern Africa, insisted that it must have been built by foreign settlers from the Mediterranean or the Middle East.

Text 2
In 1929, archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson excavated at Great Zimbabwe. She found that the pottery, tools, and other objects in the oldest layers matched those made by local African communities and that nothing in them pointed to builders from elsewhere. She concluded that the site was built by the region's own inhabitants.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A journey remembered
passages.text: In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca. His entourage spent and gave away so much gold that, according to the historian al-Umari, who visited Cairo about a dozen years later, the metal's value there had still not recovered. Accounts like al-Umari's spread Mali's reputation for wealth across North Africa and into Europe, where a 1375 Catalan atlas shows Mansa Musa holding a large piece of gold.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A defense of learning
passages.text: In 1691, the Mexican poet and scholar Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz responded to a bishop who had urged her to give up secular study. Her most famous prose work, the "Reply to Sister Philothea______ defended the right of women to pursue knowledge.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A first poem
passages.text: Phillis Wheatley, who had been brought to Boston as an enslaved child in 1761, ______ her first poem in a Rhode Island newspaper in 1767, when she was about thirteen years old.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Local, not migrant
passages.text: For decades, the naturally preserved bodies found in China's Tarim Basin puzzled researchers. Because the people had been buried with woolen clothing, wheat, and cheese, some proposed that they were migrants from far to the west. ______ a 2021 genetic study found that they descended from a long-isolated local population; their farming and herding practices had apparently spread to them without a large migration.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a notched bone
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Ishango bone was found in 1950 near the Semliki River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
- It is about 20,000 years old.
- It bears three columns of notches cut into its surface.
- Some researchers think the notches record counting or arithmetic.
- Others argue that they are simply a tally or decoration.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Early mastery
passages.text: Chauvet Cave in southern France, discovered in 1994, contains paintings of lions, rhinoceroses, and horses that radiocarbon dating places at more than 30,000 years old, roughly twice the age of the paintings at Lascaux. Yet the Chauvet artists already used shading to model their animals' bodies and overlapping outlines to suggest depth. Many scholars had assumed that cave painting developed slowly from simple to sophisticated forms. The Chauvet paintings suggest instead that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An unfinished tower
passages.text: In the early 1900s, Nikola Tesla began building Wardenclyffe Tower on Long Island, a tall structure he hoped would transmit messages, and eventually electric power, without wires. His plans for the tower remained ______: after his financier, J. P. Morgan, withdrew support, construction stopped, and the tower was torn down in 1917.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Saving the manuscripts
passages.text: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, holds hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on subjects from astronomy to law, many kept for centuries in family libraries. When armed militants occupied the city in 2012, librarians led by Abdel Kader Haidara secretly packed most of the manuscripts into footlockers and moved them to Bamako, the capital. Before leaving in early 2013, the militants set fire to several thousand manuscripts at a research institute in the city. These events suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Bee visits
passages.text:
A student counted bee visits to blue and yellow flowers in a garden on one day.
Morning: blue 48 visits, yellow 16 visits
Afternoon: blue 30 visits, yellow 30 visits
The student claims that the bees' preference for blue flowers weakened over the day.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Gardens on the lake
passages.text:
Text 1
Spanish accounts of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, described its chinampas as "floating gardens," a phrase that still appears in many modern descriptions of the city's farms.

Text 2
Archaeologists note that chinampas did not float. Farmers built them by piling layers of lake mud and decaying vegetation inside fenced plots in shallow water, then planted willow trees along the edges, whose roots anchored the plots to the lake bed. The result was fertile, stable ground surrounded by canals.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Mapping the water
passages.text: In 1887, the chemist Ellen Swallow Richards led a survey for the Massachusetts State Board of Health that analyzed tens of thousands of water samples from across the state. From the results she drew a map showing how chlorine levels in water rose near the coast and in populated areas, where sewage raised them. The map gave officials a baseline for judging whether a water supply had been polluted, and the survey led to some of the first water-quality standards in the United States.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A life in three parts
passages.text: Zora Neale Hurston's Barracoon, based on her interviews in 1927 and 1928 with Cudjo Lewis, tells the story of his life in three ______ his childhood in West Africa, his capture and transport to Alabama on the ship Clotilda, and his decades of life afterward in a community near Mobile.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Returning the bronzes
passages.text: The collection of more than 1,100 Benin Bronzes held by German museums, many of which British soldiers had taken from the royal palace in Benin City in 1897, ______ transferred to Nigerian ownership in 2022.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A rediscovered novel
passages.text: Zora Neale Hurston's novel Their Eyes Were Watching God received mixed reviews when it was published in 1937, and by the time Hurston died in 1960, it was out of print. ______ after Alice Walker's 1975 essay "In Search of Zora Neale Hurston" renewed interest in her work, the novel was reissued and became a staple of American literature courses.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A lecture and the night sky
passages.text: "When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer" is an 1865 poem by Walt Whitman. In the poem, the speaker suggests that direct experience of nature is more meaningful to him than a scientific explanation of it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A new blue
passages.text: Katsushika Hokusai's print The Great Wave off Kanagawa, made around 1831, uses large areas of Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment that had only recently become ______ in Japan: imported by Dutch and Chinese traders, it had once been too costly for most printmakers, but by the late 1820s it was cheap enough for mass-produced woodblock prints.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A misleading pattern
passages.text: The okapi, a forest animal of central Africa, was well known to local people but unknown to European zoologists until 1901. The first reports to reach Europe were based on strips of skin with bold horizontal stripes like those of a zebra, and some scientists guessed the animal was a kind of forest zebra. When a complete skin and two skulls were examined, however, the skulls' features closely matched those of giraffes. This history suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Light and fertilizer
passages.text:
A student grew bean plants with two fertilizers under two light levels and recorded the average height after four weeks.
Low light: fertilizer A 12 cm, fertilizer B 13 cm
High light: fertilizer A 20 cm, fertilizer B 28 cm
The student claims that fertilizer B's advantage over fertilizer A depended strongly on the amount of light.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two discoverers
passages.text:
Text 1
Popular accounts often present the theory of evolution by natural selection as the work of Charles Darwin alone, tracing it to his voyage on HMS Beagle and his book On the Origin of Species, published in 1859.

Text 2
In 1858, the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, working in what is now Indonesia, sent Darwin an essay describing a process of natural selection much like the one Darwin had been developing privately for years. That July, papers by both men were presented together at a meeting of the Linnean Society in London, and Darwin hurried to finish the book he published the next year.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Cards that weave
passages.text: In 1804, Joseph-Marie Jacquard patented a loom attachment that used a chain of punched cards to control which threads were raised for each pass of the shuttle, so that complex patterns could be woven automatically. Decades later, Charles Babbage planned to use similar punched cards to feed instructions and numbers into his Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculating machine that he designed but never completed.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A line on the map
passages.text: While collecting animals in the Malay Archipelago in the 1850s, Alfred Russel Wallace noticed that the islands' animals fell into two sharply different groups, one Asian and one Australian. The ______ observations of these distributions led him to propose a boundary between the two groups, now called the Wallace Line.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A letter with an almanac
passages.text: In 1791, before his first almanac was published, the self-taught astronomer and surveyor Benjamin Banneker ______ a manuscript copy of his calculations to Thomas Jefferson, along with a letter challenging Jefferson's views on race.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Words for machines
passages.text: In the early 1950s, many computer scientists assumed that computers could be programmed only in numerical code. Grace Hopper disagreed, and in 1952 she and her team completed a compiler, a program that translated instructions written in a more humanlike notation into machine code. ______ her work helped lead to COBOL, a programming language introduced in 1959 that used English words such as ADD and MOVE.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A broken wing
passages.text: "Dreams" is a 1923 poem by Langston Hughes. In the poem, the speaker suggests that life without dreams loses the ability to rise and move freely.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Reading without unrolling
passages.text: When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE, it buried a library of papyrus scrolls in the town of Herculaneum and turned them to charcoal. The carbonized scrolls are so ______ that past attempts to unroll them by hand often reduced them to fragments. In 2023, researchers instead used X-ray scans and computer analysis to read words from inside a scroll that had never been opened.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Counting touches
passages.text: The leaves of a Venus flytrap close around prey only after trigger hairs on their surface are touched twice within about twenty to thirty seconds. A single touch does not shut the trap. Researchers have also found that the plant begins producing digestive enzymes only after the trigger hairs have been touched several more times. The two-touch requirement likely helps the plant avoid ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Checking the machine
passages.text: Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at NASA whose calculations helped plan the paths of early American spaceflights. By 1962, NASA had begun using electronic computers to calculate orbits, but many astronauts did not yet fully trust them. Before his orbital flight that year, John Glenn asked that Johnson check the computer's results by hand. Her calculations matched, and the flight went ahead.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An army of clay
passages.text: Discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, the Terracotta Army, made to guard the tomb of the first emperor of China, ______ of thousands of life-size clay soldiers, each with an individually shaped face.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A first prize
passages.text: In 1950, Gwendolyn Brooks became the first Black author to win a Pulitzer ______ she received the award for Annie Allen, a collection of poems about a girl growing up in Chicago.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Many fields
passages.text: Mae Jemison became the first African American woman to travel into space when she flew aboard the space shuttle Endeavour in 1992. Her interests, however, were never limited to spaceflight. Before joining NASA, she served as a Peace Corps medical officer in Sierra Leone and Liberia. ______ after leaving NASA in 1993, she founded a technology company and taught environmental studies at Dartmouth College.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on an image
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1952, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made an X-ray image of DNA known as Photo 51.
- In 1953, Maurice Wilkins showed the image to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge.
- Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix model of DNA later in 1953.
- Franklin died in 1958.
- The 1962 Nobel Prize for the structure of DNA went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
- Under the Nobel rules of the time, a person who had died could not be nominated, and Franklin had never been nominated.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a ship
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Clotilda was the last known ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States, arriving in Alabama in 1860, decades after bringing enslaved people into the country was outlawed.
- After the voyage, the ship was burned to hide evidence of the crime.
- Many of the people it carried later founded Africatown, a community near Mobile.
- Descendants of those people still live in Africatown.
- In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Cars and camels
passages.text: In the 1920s, the naturalist Roy Chapman Andrews led a series of expeditions into Mongolia's Gobi Desert that were unusually ______: the teams traveled in automobiles, which were supplied with gasoline and food by caravans of more than one hundred camels sent ahead of them.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An egg thief?
passages.text:
Text 1
In 1924, paleontologist Henry Fairfield Osborn named a newly found dinosaur Oviraptor, meaning "egg seizer," because its skeleton lay on top of a nest of eggs that were thought to belong to another dinosaur, Protoceratops. Osborn concluded that the animal had died while raiding the nest.

Text 2
In the 1990s, researchers working in the same region found an embryo of an oviraptor-like dinosaur inside an egg of the same type. They later found oviraptorid skeletons crouched over nests with their arms spread around the eggs, in a posture much like that of brooding birds.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Counting the evidence
passages.text: In 1892, after three of her friends were murdered by a mob in Memphis, the journalist Ida B. Wells began investigating lynchings across the American South. Many white newspapers claimed that the victims had committed serious crimes. Using newspaper reports, court records, and interviews, Wells showed that in case after case the accusations were unproven or false, and she published her findings in the pamphlet Southern Horrors that year.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A first for the genre
passages.text: Octavia E. Butler, whose novels include Kindred and Parable of the Sower, ______ the first science fiction writer to receive a MacArthur Fellowship, an award often called a "genius grant," in 1995.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Never lost
passages.text: Machu Picchu, a stone city high in the Andes of Peru, was built in the mid-1400s for the Inca ruler Pachacuti and was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest a century later. ______ it was never entirely forgotten: when the American explorer Hiram Bingham arrived in 1911, local farmers were living on its terraces, and a farmer guided him there.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a fossil hunter
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Mary Anning (1799–1847) collected fossils on the cliffs near Lyme Regis, England.
- She found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile, in 1823.
- As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London.
- Scientists often bought her fossils and described them in publications without naming her.
- Today she is recognized as an important early paleontologist.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Soaking seeds
passages.text:
A student soaked bean seeds in water for different lengths of time before planting and recorded the percent that germinated.
No soaking: 40%
6 hours: 62%
12 hours: 78%
24 hours: 77%
The student claims that soaking longer than 12 hours provided no additional benefit.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lines in the desert
passages.text:
Text 1
In the mid-twentieth century, the German mathematician Maria Reiche spent decades studying the Nazca lines, huge figures and long straight lines scratched into the desert of southern Peru. She argued that many of the lines pointed to the rising and setting positions of the Sun and stars and served as an astronomical calendar.

Text 2
In 1968, the astronomer Gerald Hawkins tested this idea by comparing the directions of many lines with the positions of astronomical events. He found that the lines matched such events no more often than lines pointing in random directions would. Later researchers have proposed that the lines were paths walked in rituals, some possibly connected to water.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: How big were the ships?
passages.text: Between 1405 and 1433, the Chinese admiral Zheng He led seven great fleets across the Indian Ocean. Some Ming-era accounts describe his largest "treasure ships" as more than 400 feet long, but many historians consider those figures ______: no remains of ships that size have been found, and a wooden hull so long would have been very difficult to keep seaworthy.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Steering by stars
passages.text: Some scholars once argued that the remote islands of the Pacific were settled mostly by accident, as canoes drifted off course. In 1976, the double-hulled voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed about 2,500 miles from Hawaii to Tahiti. Its navigator, Mau Piailug, used the stars, ocean swells, and the flight of birds, without any instruments. This voyage suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Lunch and learning
passages.text:
A student compared average quiz scores in two classes before and after a school moved lunch earlier in the day.
Class A: before 74, after 75
Class B: before 70, after 79
The student claims that the schedule change was followed by a much larger improvement in class B than in class A.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The fall of a city
passages.text:
Text 1
Cahokia, a large city built by Mississippian people near present-day St. Louis, was largely abandoned by about 1350. One widely repeated explanation held that residents cut down the surrounding forests for fuel and building, causing erosion and floods that ruined the city's farmland.

Text 2
In 2021, a team led by archaeologist Caitlin Rankin examined soil layers beneath one of Cahokia's earthen mounds. They found no layers of flood sediment from the period when the city was occupied, and the ground surface remained stable until well after people had left.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Slow mail
passages.text: In the 1760s, Benjamin Franklin, then a deputy postmaster for the British colonies, wondered why mail ships from England took about two weeks longer to cross the Atlantic than many merchant ships. His cousin Timothy Folger, a whaling captain, explained that American sailors knew of a strong current flowing east and avoided sailing against it, while the mail ships' captains did not. Franklin later had a chart of the current, which he called the Gulf Stream, printed for sea captains.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Red skies
passages.text: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, a volcanic island in what is now Indonesia, had effects that reached far beyond the ______ fine ash thrown into the upper atmosphere produced vividly colored sunsets around the world for months afterward.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Leaving the Plains
passages.text: Years of drought and dust storms during the 1930s drove many families off their farms. By 1940, roughly 2.5 million people had moved out of the Plains states, many of ______ headed west to California in search of work.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: More than one role
passages.text: Harriet Tubman is best known for guiding enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad. ______ during the Civil War she served the Union Army as a scout and spy, and in 1863 she helped lead a raid along South Carolina's Combahee River that freed more than 700 people.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on the mills
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1830s and 1840s, the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, employed thousands of young women.
- Workers commonly labored about 12 to 13 hours a day.
- From 1840 to 1845, workers published The Lowell Offering, a magazine of their own writing.
- In 1834, workers walked out to protest a cut in wages.
- In 1836, workers walked out again to protest higher charges for company boardinghouses.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Poems for passengers
passages.text: After high school, Paul Laurence Dunbar, the son of formerly enslaved parents, ran the single elevator in an office building in Dayton, Ohio. He wrote poems between trips and in 1893 paid to have his first collection, Oak and Ivy, printed. The ______ passengers became some of his first readers, buying copies for a dollar each.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Pillars before farms
passages.text: Göbekli Tepe, a site in southeastern Türkiye whose massive carved stone pillars were raised more than 11,000 years ago, has ______ a long-held assumption. Many archaeologists had thought that monumental building began only after people settled into farming communities, yet the site's builders appear to have been hunter-gatherers.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The counting horse
passages.text: In the early 1900s, a horse in Berlin known as Clever Hans appeared to answer arithmetic questions by tapping his hoof. In 1907, psychologist Oskar Pfungst found that Hans answered correctly when his questioner knew the answer and was visible to him. When the questioner did not know the answer, or stood out of the horse's sight, the horse's answers were mostly wrong. These results suggest that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Where the poison comes from
passages.text: Poison dart frogs of Central and South America carry powerful toxins in their skin. A biologist claims that the frogs do not make these toxins themselves but instead obtain them from the insects and other small animals they eat in the wild.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The vine that ate the South?
passages.text:
Text 1
Kudzu, a climbing vine brought to the United States from Asia, is often called "the vine that ate the South." Popular accounts have claimed that it covers millions of acres in the southeastern states and keeps spreading rapidly across the region's forests.

Text 2
Writer Bill Finch has pointed out that U.S. Forest Service surveys found kudzu occupying only about 227,000 acres, a tiny fraction of the region's forested land. Kudzu grows best in sunny places, such as along roadsides and the edges of clearings, Finch notes, which are exactly where travelers are most likely to see it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A lake that exhaled
passages.text: In August 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon suddenly released an enormous cloud of carbon dioxide. Heavier than air, the gas flowed down into nearby valleys and killed about 1,700 people. Investigators found that carbon dioxide from volcanic sources beneath the lake had been dissolving into its deep water for years until the water could hold no more. Since 2001, engineers have installed pipes that carry deep water to the surface, allowing the gas to escape gradually.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A giant of the northern seas
