passages.text: Described by the naturalist Georg Steller in 1741, Steller's sea cow was a giant relative of the manatee that could reach about 30 feet in ______ for its meat, it was extinct within 27 years of its discovery by Europeans.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The same face
passages.text: In the 1910s and 1920s, the Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov reportedly showed audiences the same close-up of an actor's expressionless face after shots of a bowl of soup, a child in a coffin, and a woman resting on a couch. Viewers praised the actor's subtle portrayal of hunger, grief, and desire. ______ the face itself had not changed at all; the viewers' impressions came entirely from the shots placed before it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on an engineer
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Mary Golda Ross (1908–2008) was a citizen of the Cherokee Nation.
- She is often described as the first known Native American woman engineer.
- She was the only woman among the founding engineers of Lockheed's Skunk Works, a secret aerospace design group.
- She worked on studies of spaceflight, including missions to Mars and Venus.
- In 2019, she was pictured on a U.S. Native American $1 coin.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Feeder visits
passages.text:
A student counted the birds that visited a feeder in the hour after sunrise on four mornings. On two mornings the feeder held sunflower seed, and on two it held millet.
Sunflower: 34 visits and 30 visits
Millet: 12 visits and 16 visits
The student claims that the birds strongly preferred sunflower seed to millet.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A new star
passages.text: Before 1572, most European astronomers held that the heavens beyond the Moon were ______: weather and seasons might change on Earth, but the stars were thought to remain exactly as they had always been. That November, the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe observed a brilliant new star in the constellation Cassiopeia and showed, through careful measurements, that it lay far beyond the Moon.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Young forests
passages.text: Kirtland's warblers nest almost exclusively in young stands of jack pine, typically between about 5 and 20 years old, growing on sandy soils in northern Michigan. In the past, wildfires regularly cleared old jack pine forests, and new stands sprang up in their place. During the twentieth century, as people increasingly put out wildfires, young stands became scarce, and in 1974 surveyors counted only about 167 singing males. Since then, managers have harvested and replanted thousands of acres of jack pine each year. Based on the text, this approach is most likely intended to ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shade on the street
passages.text:
On a summer afternoon, a student measured the average surface temperature of sidewalks on three types of streets in her city.
No trees: 48°C
A few trees: 41°C
Continuous tree canopy: 33°C
The student claims that the drop in temperature between streets with a few trees and streets with a continuous canopy was larger than the drop between streets with no trees and streets with a few trees.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A purposeful retreat
passages.text: From 1845 to 1847, Henry David Thoreau lived in a small cabin he had built near Walden Pond in Massachusetts, an experience he described in Walden (1854). Thoreau presents his stay as a purposeful experiment, undertaken to discover what life, reduced to its essentials, could teach him.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Left and right
passages.text: In 1956, physicists Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang proposed that a long-accepted principle, that nature makes no distinction between left and right, might not hold for certain particle interactions. Later that year, the physicist Chien-Shiung Wu designed an experiment using cobalt-60 atoms cooled to near absolute zero and found that the atoms emitted electrons more often in one direction than the other, showing that the principle did fail. Lee and Yang received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics; Wu was not included.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Tall and light
passages.text: In the 1960s, the structural engineer Fazlur Khan developed the "tube" system, in which a building's closely spaced outer columns work together like a hollow tube to resist the wind. The system made very tall buildings far cheaper to construct, and Khan used versions of it in two of Chicago's best-known ______ the John Hancock Center and the Sears Tower (now the Willis Tower).
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A school far from home
passages.text: In 1900, the Yankton Dakota writer Zitkala-Ša published essays in the Atlantic Monthly about the boarding school she had attended as a child, where Native students were pressured to give up their languages and customs. ______ she recalled being forced to have her long hair cut, which in her community was associated with mourners or cowards.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A map of the world in clay
passages.text: Among the oldest known attempts to map the whole world ______ the Babylonian Map of the World, a small clay tablet from about the sixth century BCE that shows the city of Babylon surrounded by a circular ocean.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Jumping genes
passages.text: In the 1940s and 1950s, the geneticist Barbara McClintock found evidence that some genes in maize could move from one position on a chromosome to another. For years, many biologists were slow to accept her findings. In the 1970s, however, researchers found such "jumping genes" in bacteria and many other organisms, and McClintock's work was ______: in 1983, she received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The way home
passages.text: Female loggerhead sea turtles often return to nest on or near the beaches where they hatched, sometimes after decades at sea. Each stretch of coastline has a slightly different magnetic signature, determined by the strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field there. Analyzing 19 years of nesting records from Florida, biologists J. Roger Brothers and Kenneth Lohmann found that nesting sites shifted along the coast in step with small, gradual drifts in Earth's magnetic field. This finding suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Card holders
passages.text:
A student compared the number of library card holders at two branches of a city library.
Eastside: 1,200 in 2019; 1,500 in 2023
Westside: 600 in 2019; 1,200 in 2023
The student claims that Westside's number of card holders grew at a faster rate than Eastside's, even though Eastside still had more card holders in 2023.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Who came first?
passages.text:
Text 1
For much of the twentieth century, many archaeologists held that the first people to reach the Americas belonged to the Clovis culture, known from distinctive stone spear points about 13,000 years old. Under this view, no site in the Americas should be much older than the Clovis sites.

Text 2
At Monte Verde in southern Chile, a team led by archaeologist Tom Dillehay excavated wooden structures, stone tools, and food remains that radiocarbon dating placed at about 14,500 years old. In 1997, a group of archaeologists, including several who had doubted the site, visited Monte Verde and agreed that its age was well established.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Clean hands
passages.text: In 1847, the physician Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that women giving birth in a Vienna hospital ward staffed by doctors died of fever far more often than those in a ward staffed by midwives. Suspecting that doctors, who often came directly from performing autopsies, were carrying something deadly on their hands, he required them to wash with a chlorine solution, and deaths in their ward dropped sharply. Many physicians rejected his conclusion, and he died in 1865 with his ideas still widely dismissed. Only after scientists such as Louis Pasteur showed that germs cause disease did hand washing become standard medical practice.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Apartment builders
passages.text: Sociable weavers, small birds of southern Africa, build enormous communal nests of grass and twigs in trees and on telephone poles, with separate chambers for many pairs of birds. Built and expanded over many years, ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Seeing in the dark
passages.text: Most bats find their way in the dark by echolocation, producing high-pitched calls and listening for the echoes. Large fruit bats of the genus Pteropus, ______ do not echolocate; they rely mainly on their keen eyesight and sense of smell to find fruit and flowers.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A harsh nursery
passages.text: Lake Natron in northern Tanzania is so salty and alkaline that its water can burn the skin and eyes of most animals. ______ the lake is the most important breeding site in East Africa for lesser flamingos, which build their nests on islands of salt that form in its shallow waters.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on the speed of light
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1670s, Danish astronomer Ole Rømer studied eclipses of Io, one of Jupiter's moons.
- The eclipses happened later than predicted when Earth was farther from Jupiter.
- They happened earlier than predicted when Earth was closer to Jupiter.
- In 1676, Rømer concluded that light takes time to travel across space.
- Before then, many scientists believed that light traveled instantly.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A writing system
passages.text: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith, completed a writing system for the Cherokee language in 1821. Each of the system's symbols, with a single exception, ______ a syllable, which made it unusually quick to learn: within a few years, thousands of Cherokee people could read and write in their own language.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Notes on a kitchen discovery
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In the 1880s, scientists growing bacteria often used gelatin as a solid surface.
- Gelatin melts at warm temperatures, and some bacteria break it down.
- Fanny Hesse, who assisted her husband, the physician Walther Hesse, in his laboratory, suggested using agar instead.
- She had used agar to make jellies in her kitchen.
- Agar stays solid at body temperature, and few bacteria can break it down.
- Agar is still widely used to grow bacteria in laboratories.
passages.author: ai:claude
